Revelation 14:9–10 describes receiving it as an act of worship, and Revelation 13:15–18 places it within a broader system of deception, persecution, and blasphemous authority. Therefore, a cashless system might provide technological means for economic control, but it cannot be confidently identified as the mark without the surrounding biblical realities.

Faithful Christians differ on how Revelation’s symbols unfold. Futuristic interpreters expect a still-future global system involving the beast, while preterist, idealist, and historicist interpreters see varying degrees of first-century fulfillment and recurring patterns of oppressive power. These are non-essential eschatological differences, and Christians should not divide over predictions about particular technologies.

I would resist both careless speculation and complacency. Jesus calls His people to remain watchful and faithful, not fearful: “Therefore keep watch, because you do not know the day or the hour” (Matthew 25:13). The central question is not whether one possesses cash, cryptocurrency, or a digital account, but whether one belongs to Jesus Christ. He died for sinners, was buried, and rose bodily on the third day, and He will return to judge and renew all things (1 Corinthians 15:3–4; Revelation 21:1–5).

Use discernment, avoid sensational predictions, and faithfully follow Christ in your local church while awaiting His return.

question: I am a former Catholic. Should I continue to go to Catholic Church so I can reach people for Christ?
What does the Bible say about world missions?
answer:
The Bible presents world missions as God’s purpose to gather worshipers from every nation through the proclamation of the gospel of Jesus Christ. Missions is not merely cultural improvement or humanitarian work, though Christian mercy matters greatly; its central task is making disciples, planting churches, and calling sinners to repentance and faith in Christ.

**God’s heart for all nations appears throughout Scripture.** God promised Abraham, “all the families of the earth” would be blessed through him:

> “And through you all the families of the earth will be blessed.”  
> **Genesis 12:3**

The Psalms look forward to the nations worshiping the true God:

> “May God be gracious to us and bless us, and cause His face to shine upon us, that Your ways may be known on earth, Your salvation among all nations.”  
> **Psalm 67:1–2**

This promise reaches its fulfillment in Jesus Christ, the promised offspring of Abraham, and in the gathering of redeemed people from every people group.

**Jesus gave His church the Great Commission.**

> “All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to Me. Therefore go and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, and teaching them to obey all that I have commanded you. And surely I am with you always, even to the end of the age.”  
> **Matthew 28:18–20**

World missions therefore includes:

- proclaiming Christ’s death and bodily resurrection,
- calling people to repent and believe,
- baptizing believers,
- teaching obedience to all Christ commanded,
- establishing faithful local churches.

The apostles understood this mission to extend outward from Jerusalem to the whole world:

> “But you will receive power when the Holy Spirit comes upon you, and you will be My witnesses in Jerusalem, and in all Judea and Samaria, and to the ends of the earth.”  
> **Acts 1:8**

The gospel is necessary because all people are sinners and need reconciliation with God. Salvation is found in Christ alone, through grace alone, by faith alone, because of His penal substitutionary death and victorious resurrection. Paul explains why gospel messengers must be sent:

> “How then can they call on the One they have not believed in? And how can they believe in the One of whom they have not heard? And how can they hear without someone to preach? And how can they preach unless they are sent? As it is written: ‘How beautiful are the feet of those who bring good news!’”  
> **Romans 10:14–15**

Missions belongs to the whole church, not only to those who travel overseas. Churches send and support missionaries, believers pray, give, welcome international neighbors, serve sacrificially, and bear witness wherever God has placed them. In Acts, the church worshiped, fasted, prayed, and then sent workers:

> “While they were worshiping the Lord and fasting, the Holy Spirit said, ‘Set apart for Me Barnabas and Saul for the work to which I have called them.’ Then after they had fasted and prayed, they laid their hands on them and sent them off.”  
> **Acts 13:2–3**

The goal of missions is God’s glory among the nations:

> “After this I looked and saw a multitude too large to count, from every nation and tribe and people and tongue, standing before the throne and before the Lamb. They were wearing white robes and holding palm branches in their hands. And they cried out in a loud voice: ‘Salvation to our God, who sits on the throne, and to the Lamb!’”  
> **Revelation 7:9–10**

A concrete beginning would be to pray regularly for an unreached people group, support a faithful missionary or church-planting ministry, and look for opportunities to speak about Christ lovingly in your own community. Ask your local church elders how you can participate in its mission, whether by going, sending, praying, or welcoming.

question: How should we live our lives in light of our identity in Christ?
answer:
Because believers are united to Christ, we should live from our new identity rather than trying to earn one. In Christ, we are justified by grace through faith, adopted as God’s children, indwelt by the Holy Spirit, and being progressively sanctified into Christlikeness.

**1. Remember who you are.**  
Your standing before God rests on Christ’s finished work, not your performance. “Therefore, there is now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus” (Romans 8:1). This gives humility, because salvation is entirely grace, and confidence, because Christ’s righteousness is sufficient.

**2. Put sin to death and pursue holiness.**  
Union with Christ means that the old life no longer defines us. “Put to death, therefore, the components of your earthly nature” and put on the new self, “which is being renewed in knowledge in the image of its Creator” (Colossians 3:5, 10). We do not fight sin to become accepted. We fight sin because, in Christ, we have been accepted and made alive.

Practically, confess sin quickly, avoid situations that nourish it, fill your mind with Scripture, and seek accountable fellowship. Sanctification is the Spirit’s gracious work, yet we actively obey in dependence upon Him.

**3. Let love govern your relationships.**  
Christ’s people are marked by love, forgiveness, patience, and truth. “Therefore, as the elect of God, holy and beloved, clothe yourselves with compassion, kindness, humility, gentleness, and patience” (Colossians 3:12). Forgive others as the Lord forgave you, while still confronting serious sin wisely and truthfully.

**4. Live as a distinct people in the world.**  
We belong to Christ, so our values and conduct should not be shaped by the spirit of the age. Jesus says, “You are the light of the world” (Matthew 5:14). Our holiness should not be self-righteous or withdrawn, but visibly good, truthful, merciful, and ready to point others to Christ.

**5. Serve faithfully in your calling.**  
“Whatever you do, work at it with your whole being, as to the Lord and not to men” (Colossians 3:23). Work, family responsibilities, study, church service, and ordinary acts of kindness can all become worship when offered to Christ.

**6. Walk in dependence, not self-reliance.**  
Jesus said, “Apart from Me you can do nothing” (John 15:5). Remain in Him through Scripture, prayer, fellowship, the Lord’s Supper, and faithful participation in a local church. These are means through which God strengthens His people.

**7. Hope in the future Christ has secured.**  
Your identity is not finally determined by your past, present weakness, public reputation, or earthly success. “When Christ, who is your life, appears, then you also will appear with Him in glory” (Colossians 3:4). Therefore, persevere with joy, knowing that God “who began a good work in you will continue to perfect it until the day of Christ Jesus” (Philippians 1:6).

A simple pattern is: **believe what God has declared about you in Christ, put away what contradicts that identity, and put on conduct that reflects Christ’s character**. This week, read Colossians 3:1–17 slowly each day, asking the Lord to reveal one sin to put off and one Christlike virtue to put on.

question: How do I know the Bible is not just mythology?
answer:
It is reasonable to ask this. Many people wonder whether the Bible is a collection of legends, especially because it contains miracles, ancient events, and writings from many different authors. The Bible, however, is not written as mythology in the usual sense. It presents itself as a unified collection of historical testimony, prophecy, poetry, wisdom, letters, and apocalyptic literature, and its central claims are rooted in real places, rulers, people, and events.

Several considerations support its trustworthiness:

- **The Bible claims historical investigation and eyewitness testimony.** Luke says he carefully investigated the events so that his reader could know their certainty, and Peter says the apostles did not follow “cleverly devised fables” but were eyewitnesses of Christ’s majesty (Luke 1:1–4; 2 Peter 1:16).
- **Its central message is not detached from history.** Christianity stands or falls on Jesus Christ’s actual death, burial, and bodily resurrection. Paul names specific eyewitnesses, many of whom were still living when he wrote (1 Corinthians 15:3–8). This is very different from a timeless “once upon a time” myth.
- **Its writings show remarkable unity amid real diversity.** Across centuries, authors from different backgrounds consistently testify that humanity is sinful, God is holy, redemption is necessary, and salvation culminates in Jesus Christ.
- **Its manuscript tradition is substantial.** We possess many ancient copies and quotations of the biblical writings, allowing the text to be carefully compared and reconstructed. This does not prove that every miracle occurred, but it does mean the question is not whether we have any idea what the biblical authors wrote.
- **The Bible’s message is spiritually self-authenticating.** Christians do not believe merely because of external evidence, but because God opens the heart to recognize the truth and glory of His Word, especially in Christ (1 Corinthians 2:12–14; 2 Corinthians 4:6).

Evidence can show that belief in the Bible is reasonable, but saving faith is not produced by evidence alone. The deepest issue is not merely, “Is this text ancient?” but, “Will I receive what God says about me and about His Son?” The Bible exposes human sin and our separation from a holy God, but it also announces that Jesus, truly God and truly man, lived without sin, died as a substitute for sinners, was buried, and rose bodily on the third day. Salvation is by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone, not by moral effort (Romans 3:23–26; Ephesians 2:8–9).

A good next step is to read one of the Gospels, especially Luke or John, asking God to help you see whether Jesus is truly who the Bible says He is. Turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose again for forgiveness and new life.

question: What does it mean that the Bible is infallible? What is biblical infallibility?
answer:
Biblical infallibility means that the Bible, because it is the Word breathed out by God, cannot fail, deceive, or lead God’s people astray in all that it teaches. Scripture is wholly trustworthy and carries God’s own authority.

Paul writes, **“All Scripture is God-breathed and is useful for instruction, for conviction, for correction, and for training in righteousness”** (2 Timothy 3:16). Because God is true and does not lie, His written Word is dependable: **“God is not a man, that He should lie”** (Numbers 23:19); **“Your word is truth”** (John 17:17).

“Infallible” emphasizes that Scripture **cannot fail**. “Inerrant” emphasizes that Scripture **does not contain error** in its original writings. The terms are closely related: because God is the truthful Author, His Word is both infallible and inerrant. Jesus treated the Scriptures as completely authoritative, saying, **“the Scripture cannot be broken”** (John 10:35).

This does not mean that every biblical passage is written in the same style or should be read in a woodenly literal way. Poetry uses imagery, parables communicate through stories, and historical narrative reports events as history. Infallibility means that each passage is true according to its literary form and intended meaning. Nor does it mean that every later manuscript copy or translation is perfect in the same sense as the original writings. God has preserved His Word faithfully, though textual study recognizes minor copyist differences that do not overturn Christian doctrine.

Biblical infallibility therefore means:

- The Bible is inspired by God.
- The Bible is completely truthful in what it teaches.
- The Bible cannot ultimately fail in its purpose.
- The Bible is the final authority for faith and practice.
- The Bible is sufficient to make God’s people wise for salvation and equipped for godly living (2 Timothy 3:15–17).

This is not merely an academic doctrine. If Scripture is infallible, we should receive it humbly, test our beliefs by it, and obey it even when it corrects our desires or assumptions. As Psalm 119:160 says, **“The entirety of Your word is truth, and every one of Your righteous judgments endures forever.”**

question: What does the Bible mean when it says something is unclean?
answer:
In the Bible, **“unclean” means unsuitable for God’s holy presence or for a holy purpose**. The meaning depends on context: it can describe **ceremonial impurity**, **moral sin**, or an **unclean spirit**.

In the Old Testament, many things made a person ceremonially unclean, including certain diseases, bodily discharges, contact with a corpse, and eating forbidden animals. This did not always mean the person had committed a moral sin. Rather, it made the person temporarily unable to participate in Israel’s worship until cleansed according to God’s appointed instructions. These laws taught Israel that God is holy and that sinners cannot casually approach Him. See Leviticus 11:44–45; Leviticus 15:31; Numbers 19:11–13.

The Bible also uses “unclean” in a **moral sense**, referring to practices that defile a person before God, especially sexual immorality, idolatry, and corrupt desires. This kind of uncleanness is sin, not merely ritual impurity. See Leviticus 18:24–30; Ephesians 5:3–5; Colossians 3:5–6.

In the New Testament, Jesus taught that true defilement comes from the sinful heart:

> “Nothing that enters a man from the outside can defile him, but the things that come out of a man are what defile him.”  
> Mark 7:15

He then identifies sins such as evil thoughts, sexual immorality, theft, murder, adultery, greed, deceit, and pride as things that defile a person. See Mark 7:20–23.

This does not mean that the Old Testament laws were meaningless. They pointed forward to Christ and showed the need for deeper cleansing. In Christ, believers are cleansed from sin through His **atoning sacrifice**, and they are progressively made holy through **sanctification** by the Holy Spirit. See Hebrews 9:13–14; Titus 3:5; 1 John 1:7–9.

“Unclean spirits” refers to evil spirits opposed to God, also called demons. Jesus’ authority over them displays His divine lordship and His victory over Satan’s kingdom. See Mark 1:23–27; Luke 11:20.

So, when you encounter “unclean,” ask:

1. Is this referring to ceremonial impurity under the Old Covenant?
2. Is it describing sinful behavior or a defiled heart?
3. Is it referring to an evil spirit?

For Christians today, the central question is not merely external cleanliness but whether we have been cleansed from sin through faith in Jesus Christ. Turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died on the cross and rose bodily from the grave to forgive sinners and give them new life.

question: What is the meaning of life?
answer:
The meaning of life is to know, love, and glorify God, and to enjoy Him forever through Jesus Christ. We were created in God’s image for fellowship with Him and faithful stewardship of His world, not for temporary achievements alone (Genesis 1:27–28; Ecclesiastes 12:13; Matthew 22:37–39).

Sin has separated humanity from our holy Creator, so pleasure, success, and self-definition cannot finally satisfy us (Romans 3:23; Ecclesiastes 2:10–11). But God sent His Son, Jesus Christ, who became truly man while remaining truly God, lived without sin, died on the cross as the substitute for sinners, was buried, and bodily rose on the third day (1 Corinthians 15:3–4; 2 Corinthians 5:21). In Him, life receives forgiveness, reconciliation with God, a new purpose, and the hope of resurrection and eternal life.

Jesus said, “I have come that they may have life, and have it in all its fullness” (John 10:10). The Christian’s purpose, then, is to abide in Christ, grow in holiness, love others, proclaim the gospel, and serve God faithfully in every calling (John 15:4–5; Ephesians 2:10; Matthew 28:18–20).

Turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose for forgiveness and new life. A practical place to begin is to read the Gospel of John slowly, asking God to show you who Jesus is and how you should respond.

question: How can there be subordination in the Trinity?
answer:
There can be **subordination in the Trinity with respect to role and relation, but never with respect to deity, glory, or being**. The Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one God, possessing the same divine nature, while personally distinguished as Father, Son, and Spirit.

The Son’s submission to the Father is especially clear in His incarnate mission. The Father sends the Son, and the Son willingly obeys the Father, even unto death: “I have come down from heaven, not to do My own will, but to do the will of Him who sent Me” (John 6:38). In His humanity, Jesus prays, “Not My will, but Yours be done” (Luke 22:42), and “He humbled Himself and became obedient to death” (Philippians 2:8).

Yet this obedience does not mean that the Son is less divine or eternally inferior to the Father. Jesus also says, “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30), and the Jews understood His claim as making Himself equal with God (John 5:18). The Son is “the image of the invisible God” and “the exact representation of His nature” (Colossians 1:15; Hebrews 1:3). The historic term for this truth is the **hypostatic union**: Jesus Christ is one Person with a truly divine nature and a truly human nature.

The Spirit likewise proceeds from the Father and is sent by the Father and the Son in the work of redemption (John 15:26; John 16:7), yet He is fully divine, not a lesser being. Ananias’s lie to the Holy Spirit is called a lie to God (Acts 5:3–4).

So we should distinguish:

- **Ontological equality:** The three Persons are equally God, eternal, holy, omnipotent, and worthy of worship.
- **Personal distinction:** The Father is not the Son, the Son is not the Spirit, and the Spirit is not the Father.
- **Economic or mission-based order:** The Father sends, the Son accomplishes redemption, and the Spirit applies redemption.
- **Voluntary submission:** The Son’s obedience is not forced inferiority but the loving fulfillment of His saving mission.

When Paul says that “the Son Himself will be made subject to Him who put all things under Him” (1 Corinthians 15:28), he is speaking of the Son’s ordered kingdom and completed mediatorial mission, not saying that the Son ceases to be fully God. The Son remains eternally worthy of the same honor as the Father: “that all may honor the Son just as they honor the Father” (John 5:23).

Thus, there is **order without inequality, submission without inferiority, and distinction without division**. The Trinity is not a hierarchy of gods, but one God in three eternally distinct Persons.

question: Why are there so many religions? Do all religions lead to God?
answer:
There are many religions because humanity is made by God yet separated from Him by sin, and people seek answers about God, guilt, meaning, death, and worship in different cultures and ways. The Bible teaches that God has made Himself known through creation and conscience, but that fallen humanity often suppresses or distorts that truth, turning to idols and human traditions, Romans 1:18–25.

Christians should respect people of every background, but Christianity does not teach that all religions are equally true or that all paths lead to God. Jesus made an exclusive claim: **“I am the way and the truth and the life. No one comes to the Father except through Me”** (John 14:6). Scripture also says, **“There is salvation in no one else”** (Acts 4:12), and identifies Jesus as the one mediator between God and humanity, 1 Timothy 2:5.

This is not because Christians are morally better than others. All people, including Christians, are sinners who need mercy, Romans 3:10–12, 23. The difference is that Christianity proclaims what God has done in Christ: Jesus, truly God and truly man, lived without sin, died on the cross as a substitute for sinners, was buried, and rose bodily on the third day, 1 Corinthians 15:3–4; 2 Corinthians 5:21. We are justified by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone, not by religious works, Ephesians 2:8–9; Romans 5:1.

So the Christian answer is: **No, all religions do not lead to God.** Religious sincerity cannot remove sin, but Christ is a perfectly sufficient Savior. Turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose for forgiveness and new life.

Is your question mainly about the fairness of God’s judgment, or about whether Jesus’ claim to be the only way is true?

question: Do Mormons believe in the Trinity?
answer:
No. **The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints (LDS)** uses the phrase “Godhead,” but it does not affirm the historic Christian doctrine of the Trinity. LDS teaching describes the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit as **three separate beings**, united in purpose, rather than one God eternally existing in three distinct persons and one divine essence.

Historic Christianity teaches that there is **one God in three persons**, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. This is reflected in passages such as Matthew 28:19, John 1:1, and 2 Corinthians 13:14. Jesus Christ is not merely a separate divine being or created spirit, but truly God and truly man, the eternal Son who took on human nature.

This distinction is a core doctrinal difference, not merely a difference in terminology. We should speak of LDS people with kindness and respect, while clearly recognizing that LDS theology is outside historic orthodox Christianity on the Trinity and the deity of Christ.

question: Where is the moral law summarily comprehended?
answer: The moral law is **summarily comprehended in the Ten Commandments**. Jesus further summarizes its heart as loving God wholly and loving your neighbor as yourself, Matthew 22:37–40; Romans 13:8–10.

question: What does it mean to be contrite? What is contrition?
answer:
To be **contrite** means to be genuinely humbled and brokenhearted over your sin before God. **Contrition** is the sorrow that recognizes, “I have sinned against a holy and good God,” rather than merely regretting the consequences of being caught.

David expressed this kind of repentance after his sin:

> “The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit; a broken and contrite heart, O God, You will not despise.”  
> **Psalm 51:17**

Contrition is not hopeless self-hatred or trying to punish yourself. It is honest sorrow that turns toward God for mercy. Biblical sorrow leads to repentance, while worldly sorrow may only produce shame or despair: **2 Corinthians 7:10**. God promises to receive the humble and repentant:

> “This is the one I will esteem: he who is humble and contrite in spirit, who trembles at My word.”  
> **Isaiah 66:2**

In Christian theology, contrition is part of **repentance**, but it is not what earns forgiveness. We are justified by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone. Jesus bore the guilt of His people in His substitutionary death and rose bodily from the grave, so those who confess their sins and trust in Him receive forgiveness: **1 John 1:9**; **Romans 3:23–26**.

A practical expression of contrition is to name the sin honestly before God, stop defending it, ask for forgiveness, and take a concrete step away from it while trusting Christ rather than your own sorrow.

question: What does it mean that “at your right hand are pleasures forevermore” (Psalm 16:11)?
answer:
Psalm 16:11 means that **true and lasting joy is found in God’s presence**, not in temporary earthly pleasures. David says:

> “You have made known to me the path of life; You will fill me with joy in Your presence, with eternal pleasures at Your right hand.”  
> Psalm 16:11

“Your right hand” is biblical language for God’s **power, favor, and honored presence**. To be at God’s right hand is to enjoy the highest blessing and security that God gives. The “pleasures” are not sinful indulgence, but the pure, complete, and enduring delight found in knowing God Himself. They are “forevermore,” unlike earthly joys, which fade or are mixed with sorrow.

The immediate context shows that this joy comes through trusting God:

> “I have set the LORD always before me. Because He is at my right hand, I will not be shaken.”  
> Psalm 16:8

The New Testament also treats Psalm 16 as pointing ultimately to Jesus Christ. Peter applies it to Christ’s bodily resurrection in Acts 2:25–32, and Paul does likewise in Acts 13:35–37. Jesus entered death, rose bodily, and was exalted to the Father’s right hand, where fullness of joy is found. This connects Psalm 16:11 with the Christian hope of resurrection and eternal communion with God, not merely present emotional happiness.

For believers, the verse is both a promise and a direction: God does not merely give us gifts, He gives us Himself. We may experience real joy with Him now through Christ, Scripture, prayer, and fellowship, and one day we will enjoy His presence without sin, sorrow, or death. Set aside time today to bring both your gratitude and your deepest longings directly to God, asking Him to teach you to desire His presence above passing pleasures.

question: What is divine providence?
answer:
Divine providence is God’s continual, wise, holy, and loving work by which He preserves His creation, governs all events, and directs them toward His appointed purposes. Nothing happens outside His knowledge, authority, or sustaining power, yet God remains righteous and human beings remain genuinely responsible for their choices.

Scripture says, “He is before all things, and in Him all things hold together” (Colossians 1:17), and, “Our God is in heaven; He does as He pleases” (Psalm 115:3). God’s providence includes:

- **Preservation:** He sustains the existence of all things (Hebrews 1:3).
- **Government:** He rules over nations, rulers, ordinary events, and the course of history (Daniel 4:35; Proverbs 16:9).
- **God’s use of means:** He ordinarily works through prayer, work, relationships, wisdom, and natural processes, while remaining free to act miraculously (James 1:5; Philippians 2:12–13).
- **His purpose in suffering:** God is never the author of sin, but He can govern even grievous events for good. The clearest example is Joseph’s words concerning his brothers: “You intended to harm me, but God intended it for good” (Genesis 50:20). At the cross, wicked human actions were truly sinful, yet God’s saving purpose was fulfilled (Acts 2:23).

This doctrine is closely related to **God’s sovereignty**, but providence emphasizes His active, ongoing care and governance of creation. It is not fatalism. Fatalism says events occur through impersonal necessity; providence says the personal God wisely and purposefully upholds and directs all things.

For believers, providence is not meant to produce passivity but trust and obedience. We pray, act wisely, and pursue holiness because God works through these means, while resting in His promise: “And we know that God works all things together for the good of those who love Him, who are called according to His purpose” (Romans 8:28). A practical response is to bring today’s uncertainties honestly to God in prayer, obey the responsibilities He has placed before you, and leave the hidden future in His wise hands.

question: In what ways is the Christian life like the Olympics?
answer:
The Christian life is like the Olympics in several important ways, though the comparison has limits:

- **It requires disciplined training.** Athletes prepare their bodies and minds, and Christians are called to train in godliness through Scripture, prayer, worship, fellowship, and obedience. “Train yourself for godliness” (1 Timothy 4:7–8).

- **It involves perseverance.** The race is not won by a promising beginning but by faithfully pressing on through hardship. “Let us run with endurance the race that lies before us” (Hebrews 12:1–2).

- **It demands focus on the goal.** Paul described his pursuit of Christ as pressing “toward the goal to win the prize of God’s heavenly calling in Christ Jesus” (Philippians 3:13–14). Christians must continually turn their attention from distractions to Christ.

- **It calls for self-control.** Olympic athletes willingly deny themselves many legitimate pleasures for the sake of competition. Likewise, believers put sin to death and pursue holiness, not to earn God’s acceptance, but because they have received grace. “Everyone who competes in the games trains with strict discipline” (1 Corinthians 9:25–27).

- **It includes hardship and sacrifice.** Training can be painful, and following Jesus includes costly obedience. Yet present suffering is not pointless, because God uses it to conform His people to Christ (Romans 8:17–18, 29).

- **It is not merely an individual event.** Athletes may compete personally, but they also belong to teams and represent others. Christians belong to the body of Christ and are called to encourage and strengthen one another (1 Corinthians 12:12–27; Hebrews 10:24–25).

- **It has an imperishable reward.** Olympic medals fade, but the reward Christ gives is eternal. “They do it to receive a perishable crown, but we do it to receive an imperishable crown” (1 Corinthians 9:25). Paul looked forward to “the crown of righteousness” given by the righteous Judge (2 Timothy 4:7–8).

The crucial difference is that Christians do **not** run in order to earn salvation. We run because Christ has already saved us by grace alone through faith alone, and He supplies the strength to persevere. The Christian race begins with faith in Christ, is sustained by His grace, and ends in His presence.

question: What should be the Christian perspective on nudity in art?
answer:
Christianity does not make every depiction of the unclothed human body automatically sinful, but it requires believers to distinguish between honest artistic representation and imagery designed to awaken or satisfy lust.

Faithful Christians differ here: some conclude that artistic nudity is never appropriate because it can violate modesty and become a stumbling block, while others believe non-erotic depictions, especially in historical, anatomical, or serious artistic contexts, may be viewed with a clear conscience.

I believe the second position can be faithful to Scripture, provided the work is not sexually provocative and the viewer is not using “art” to excuse lust. Before the fall, Adam and Eve were naked without shame, but after sin entered, nakedness became associated with shame and the need for covering (Genesis 2:25; Genesis 3:7, 21). Jesus condemns lustful intent, not merely the physical sight of another person: “Everyone who looks at a woman with lust has already committed adultery with her in his heart” (Matthew 5:28). Job’s resolve is therefore wise: “I have made a covenant with my eyes” (Job 31:1).

A Christian should ask:

- Is the work portraying the human body with dignity, or objectifying it?
- Does it invite thoughtful appreciation, or sexual desire?
- Can I view or display it with a clear conscience before God?
- Could it reasonably tempt me or another person toward lust?
- Would displaying it be loving and appropriate in this setting?

The relevant theological principles are **Christian liberty**, **modesty**, **purity**, and **love for one’s neighbor**. “Whatever is true, whatever is honorable, whatever is right, whatever is pure” should shape our attention (Philippians 4:8), and our bodies and eyes belong to the Lord (1 Corinthians 6:18–20).

As a practical step, if you feel troubled by a particular work, do not silence your conscience merely to appear sophisticated; set it aside, pray for wisdom, and seek counsel from a mature pastor or believer. Romans 14:23 teaches that “whatever is not from faith is sin.”

question: Should we allow false teachers into our home?
answer:
No. Scripture specifically warns believers not to welcome false teachers into their homes or support their ministry when they deny the truth about Christ.

> “If anyone comes to you but does not bring this teaching, do not receive him into your home or even greet him. Whoever greets such a person shares in his evil deeds.”  
> **2 John 1:10–11**

In its first-century setting, welcoming a traveling teacher into one’s home often meant offering hospitality, protection, and material support for his work. John is not forbidding ordinary kindness, respectful conversation, or evangelistic engagement with unbelievers. He is forbidding partnership that would help someone spread destructive error, especially error concerning Jesus Christ. Believers must “test the spirits” by the apostolic gospel, not accept every spiritual claim uncritically, **1 John 4:1–3**.

The Christian should therefore:

- **Refuse to host or materially support teachers who deny essential truth**, such as Christ’s deity, incarnation, bodily resurrection, or saving work.
- **Avoid giving them a platform in the church or home** under the guise of neutrality.
- **Speak truthfully and graciously**, remembering that “the Lord’s servant must not be quarrelsome but kind to everyone,” **2 Timothy 2:24–25**.
- **Remain ready to show the gospel to those who are deceived**, while distinguishing compassion for people from endorsement of false teaching.

A practical step is to ask your pastor or elders to help you evaluate the teacher’s message, especially what they say about the person and work of Jesus Christ. Protecting your household and church from spiritual deception is not unloving; it is part of faithful shepherding.

question: How is God’s Word a lamp to my feet (Psalm 119:105)?
answer:
Psalm 119:105 says, **“Your word is a lamp to my feet and a light to my path.”** God’s Word guides us in two related ways:

- **A lamp to our feet:** It gives enough light for the next faithful step, especially when circumstances are unclear. Scripture shows us what is pleasing to God, exposes sin, and gives wisdom for daily choices.
- **A light to our path:** It reveals the direction and character of the life God calls us to walk, centered on holiness, love, wisdom, and faith in Him.

The image is not of a powerful floodlight showing every detail of the future. Rather, like a small lamp used on a dark path, Scripture gives trustworthy guidance as we walk by faith. It may not answer every question with a specific command, but it gives principles, priorities, warnings, promises, and wisdom for applying God’s will.

This guidance includes conviction: **“I have hidden Your word in my heart that I might not sin against You”** (Psalm 119:11). It also includes practical wisdom: **“Make my footsteps firm in Your word; do not let any sin rule over me”** (Psalm 119:133). Ultimately, the Word points us to Jesus Christ, who is not merely a guide but **“the way and the truth and the life”** (John 14:6).

A practical way to live this verse is to read a short portion of Scripture each morning and ask: *What does this show me about God? What sin must I turn from? What promise should I trust? What obedient step should I take today?* Then follow that light, even when you cannot yet see the whole road.

question: Why were the people guilty for a priest’s sin?
answer:
In **Leviticus 4**, the people were not necessarily guilty of personally committing the priest’s sin; rather, the priest’s sin brought **corporate covenant guilt and consequences** upon Israel because he represented the nation before God.

The high priest was a spiritual representative and teacher. If he sinned in his official role, especially in a way that misled the people, his failure affected the whole covenant community:

> “If the anointed priest sins, bringing guilt on the people, he must present to the LORD a young bull without blemish as a sin offering for the sin he has committed.”  
> **Leviticus 4:3**

Likewise, if the whole congregation sinned unintentionally, a sacrifice was required for the community:

> “When the whole congregation of Israel errs unintentionally and becomes guilty by doing what is forbidden in the LORD’s commands, even though the matter escapes the assembly’s notice...”  
> **Leviticus 4:13**

This reflects the biblical principle that leaders have **representative responsibility**. Their sin can damage and implicate those entrusted to their care, though Scripture also teaches that each person is accountable for his or her own sin:

> “The soul who sins is the one who will die.”  
> **Ezekiel 18:4**

So the distinction is important: the people could suffer covenant consequences from the priest’s sin and might share in communal guilt, but God did not treat every individual as personally blameworthy for an act they neither committed nor endorsed. The sacrificial system provided atonement for the community.

This also points forward to Jesus Christ, the sinless High Priest. Unlike Israel’s priests, He did not need an offering for His own sin. He offered Himself once for all, bearing the guilt of His people through **penal substitution**:

> “Such a high priest truly meets our need, One who is holy, innocent, undefiled, set apart from sinners, and exalted above the heavens. Unlike the other high priests, He does not need to offer daily sacrifices, first for his own sins and then for the sins of the people. He sacrificed for sin once for all when He offered Himself.”  
> **Hebrews 7:26–27**

question: What is spiritual mapping?
answer:
**Spiritual mapping** is a practice used in some Christian circles to study a community’s history, beliefs, cultural influences, and social problems in order to guide prayer and evangelism. It may also include claims about identifying “territorial spirits” or demonic strongholds associated with particular places.

The Bible clearly teaches that spiritual warfare is real: “For our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against the rulers, against the authorities, against the powers of this world’s darkness, and against the spiritual forces of evil in the heavenly realms” (Ephesians 6:12). Christians should therefore pray, proclaim the gospel, resist temptation, and stand in God’s truth (Ephesians 6:10–18; 1 Peter 5:8–9).

Faithful Christians differ over whether detailed spiritual mapping is a useful evangelistic tool. Some view careful cultural research and prayer walking as applications of loving one’s neighbors and praying for the community (1 Timothy 2:1–4; Jeremiah 29:7). Others caution that Scripture does not command believers to name, map, or directly address territorial spirits, and that such practices can become speculative or distract from the ordinary means God has given: Scripture, prayer, godly fellowship, and gospel preaching. Scripture also warns against seeking hidden spiritual knowledge through forbidden practices (Deuteronomy 18:10–12).

My position is cautious: researching a community and praying for its people can be beneficial, but Christians should not treat unproven claims about territorial demons as biblical certainty. Our confidence is not in discovering secret spiritual structures, but in the reigning Christ, whose gospel is “the power of God for salvation” (Romans 1:16). A practical approach is to pray specifically for local people, churches, leaders, justice, repentance, and opportunities to speak about Jesus, while remaining anchored in Scripture and accountable to your local church elders.

question: What is God’s design for marriage?
answer:
God’s design for marriage is a lifelong covenant between one man and one woman, established by God for companionship, faithful sexual union, the raising of children, and the mutual display of Christlike love.

- **God-created companionship:** “It is not good for the man to be alone” (Genesis 2:18). Marriage answers human solitude with faithful partnership.
- **One-flesh union:** God made them male and female and joined them together so that “the two of them will become one flesh” (Genesis 2:24). This includes bodily, emotional, spiritual, and covenantal unity.
- **Lifelong covenant faithfulness:** Jesus says, “What God has joined together, let man not separate” (Matthew 19:6). Marriage is not merely a contract based on changing feelings, but a solemn covenant requiring steadfast love.
- **Fruitfulness and family:** God blessed the man and woman, saying, “Be fruitful and multiply” (Genesis 1:28). Children are a gift from the Lord, and parents are called to raise them in the instruction of the Lord (Psalm 127:3; Ephesians 6:4).
- **Mutual holiness and service:** Husband and wife are to love, honor, forgive, and serve one another. The husband is called to sacrificial headship modeled on Christ, while the wife is called to willing, respectful partnership, and both are commanded to submit to one another in reverence for Christ (Ephesians 5:21–33; 1 Peter 3:7).
- **A picture of the gospel:** Christian marriage points beyond itself to the covenant love of Christ for His church. Paul calls this a “profound mystery” concerning “Christ and the church” (Ephesians 5:31–32). In this sense, marriage can be a means of **sanctification**, teaching spouses repentance, patience, self-denial, and grace.

Marriage is therefore good, but it is not the highest human calling. Christ Himself is Lord over marriage, and a person’s worth and salvation do not depend on being married. Whether married or single, we are reconciled to God by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone, because of His atoning death and bodily resurrection (Romans 5:1; 1 Corinthians 15:3–4).

A practical place to begin is for a husband and wife to read Ephesians 5:21–33 together, asking not first, “What must my spouse do?” but, “How is Christ calling me to love, serve, repent, and remain faithful?”

question: What is the value of group Bible study?
answer:
Group Bible study is valuable because God ordinarily grows Christians through His Word in the fellowship of His people, not in isolation.

- **It strengthens understanding.** Other believers ask questions, offer insights, and help us notice the immediate context and wider teaching of Scripture. “As iron sharpens iron, so one man sharpens another” (Proverbs 27:17).
- **It encourages obedience.** Studying together moves the Bible from information to application, helping believers “be doers of the word, and not hearers only” (James 1:22).
- **It provides mutual encouragement and accountability.** Christians can pray for one another, bear burdens, and persevere in faith. Hebrews 10:24–25 calls believers to consider how to spur one another toward love and good deeds and not neglect meeting together.
- **It guards against individual error.** A humble group can test interpretations against the whole counsel of Scripture rather than allowing one person’s preferences to control the discussion. The Bereans were commended for examining the Scriptures carefully (Acts 17:11).
- **It builds Christian love and unity.** As believers learn the truth together, they grow in “the unity of the faith” and maturity in Christ (Ephesians 4:11–16).

Group study does not replace personal prayer and Scripture reading, nor does a group’s opinion outrank the Bible. Its purpose is to place believers under the authority of God’s Word together, with faithful teaching and humble discussion.

A helpful next step is to join or begin a group that studies a biblical book passage by passage, asks what the text means, how it points to Christ, and how it should shape daily obedience. A mature church elder or pastor should help oversee the study, since teachers bear greater responsibility (James 3:1).

question: How can I overcome a feeling of spiritual emptiness?
answer:
Feeling spiritually empty can be frightening and exhausting, but it does not mean God has abandoned you. Many genuine believers experience seasons of dryness, and God’s promise rests on His faithfulness, not on the intensity of your feelings: “I will never leave you, never will I forsake you” (Hebrews 13:5).

Begin by coming honestly to God rather than waiting to feel spiritually strong. Tell Him where you are, confess any known sin, and ask Him to renew your heart. Scripture says, “Draw near to God, and He will draw near to you” (James 4:8), and Jesus invites the weary to come to Him for rest (Matthew 11:28-30).

A few concrete steps may help:

- Read a short portion of Scripture slowly each day, especially Psalms, John, or Romans. Ask, “What does this show me about God, and how should I respond?” God ordinarily nourishes His people through His Word, not merely through emotional experiences (Romans 10:17).
- Keep praying even when prayer feels dry. Bring God your actual thoughts, fears, sins, and desires, and pray through a Psalm such as Psalm 42 or Psalm 63.
- Reconnect with faithful Christians and attend a sound local church. Isolation often deepens emptiness, while fellowship, preaching, communion, and mutual encouragement are ordinary means by which God strengthens His people (Hebrews 10:24-25).
- Examine whether unconfessed sin, bitterness, distraction, exhaustion, or grief is affecting you. Repentance is not earning God’s love. It is turning from sin and receiving His restoring grace (1 John 1:9).
- Serve someone in a simple, self-giving way. This does not purchase spiritual life, but it can redirect your attention from inward heaviness toward love of neighbor (Galatians 5:13).

Most importantly, spiritual emptiness cannot finally be cured by trying harder or collecting religious experiences. We are sinners separated from a holy God and need a Savior. Jesus Christ, truly God and truly man, lived without sin, died on the cross as the substitute for sinners, was buried, and rose bodily on the third day. Through His atoning death and resurrection, God justifies the ungodly by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone, giving forgiveness and new life (Romans 3:23-26; 1 Corinthians 15:3-4; Ephesians 2:8-9). Turn from your sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose for you.

If this emptiness is accompanied by persistent hopelessness, inability to function, or thoughts of harming yourself, please contact emergency services immediately if you are in danger, and speak with a qualified medical professional as well as a pastor or mature Christian counselor. Spiritual care and appropriate medical care can be pursued together.

What seems closest to your experience right now: guilt over sin, grief or suffering, doubt, loneliness, or simply a lack of spiritual feeling?

question: How can I, a Muslim, become assured of paradise?
answer:
Your desire for assurance of paradise is deeply important. Many Muslims sincerely seek Allah’s mercy through faith, repentance, prayer, and good works, yet the question remains whether anyone can know with certainty that their sins are forgiven. The Bible gives assurance not because we have earned enough merit, but because God has provided a perfect Savior.

The Bible teaches that God is holy and that all people have sinned and stand accountable before Him: “For all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God” (Romans 3:23). Good works cannot erase guilt before a just God. We need a mediator and substitute.

Christianity proclaims that Jesus Christ is more than a prophet. He is the eternal Son of God who became truly man through the virgin birth, lived without sin, and died on the cross as the **penal substitute** for sinners. He was buried and bodily raised on the third day, and He now reigns as Lord. “There is indeed one God and one mediator between God and mankind, the man Christ Jesus” (1 Timothy 2:5). “Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures, He was buried, He was raised on the third day according to the Scriptures” (1 Corinthians 15:3–4).

Therefore, assurance rests in Christ, not in the uncertain balance of our deeds: “Therefore, since we have been justified through faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ” (Romans 5:1). The apostle John says, “I have written these things to you who believe in the name of the Son of God, so that you may know that you have eternal life” (1 John 5:13). Salvation is by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone, not by works (Ephesians 2:8–9).

I respect you as someone made in God’s image, but I must be clear about the Christian claim: Jesus is the only Savior, and reconciliation with God comes through Him, not through Islam, morality, or religious effort. Turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose for you, for forgiveness and eternal life.

Would you be willing to read the Gospel of John and consider Jesus’ own words about who He is and how He gives life?

question: What is the spiritual gift of miracles?
answer:
The spiritual gift of miracles is a Holy Spirit-given ability to accomplish extraordinary works that display God’s power, serve His people, and confirm the truth of the Gospel, as described in “workings of miracles” in 1 Corinthians 12:10, 1 Corinthians 12:28.  

Continuationists argue that this gift remains available to the church today because the Holy Spirit still distributes gifts “as He sees fit,” and Scripture does not explicitly say that miracles ceased, 1 Corinthians 12:11; 1 Corinthians 14:1.  

I understand the cessationist position to be most faithful to the biblical pattern: miraculous sign-gifts were especially associated with Christ’s apostles and the foundational confirmation of their message, Hebrews 2:3–4; 2 Corinthians 12:12, though God Himself remains sovereign and may perform miracles whenever He pleases. This gift is not human magic or a guaranteed power to heal on demand. The apostles performed signs by God’s authority, while the Lord alone determined the outcome, Acts 3:12–16; Acts 14:8–15.

The proper response is humility: pray boldly for God’s help, trust His wisdom when He says “no,” and never measure faithfulness merely by visible signs. The ordinary means by which Christ builds His church remain the preached Word, prayer, fellowship, and the ordinances, Acts 2:42; Romans 10:17.

question: What does it mean that God is merciful?
answer:
God is **merciful** because He is compassionate toward people in misery and does not give sinners the judgment they deserve. Mercy is God’s loving action toward the guilty and needy, flowing from His goodness and not from anything we have earned.

Scripture says, “The LORD is compassionate and gracious, slow to anger, abounding in loving devotion” (Psalm 103:8). It also declares, “He does not treat us as our sins deserve or repay us according to our iniquities” (Psalm 103:10).

God’s mercy does not mean that He ignores or overlooks sin. He is perfectly holy and just. Rather, at the cross, justice and mercy meet: Jesus Christ bore the judgment deserved by His people as a **penal substitution**, and God freely forgives those who trust in Him. “But because of His great love for us, God, who is rich in mercy, made us alive with Christ even when we were dead in our trespasses” (Ephesians 2:4–5).

For believers, God’s mercy means you can come to Him honestly in repentance, even after failure, because He welcomes the brokenhearted. “Let us then approach the throne of grace with confidence, so that we may receive mercy and find grace to help us in our time of need” (Hebrews 4:16). A practical response is to confess your sin directly to God, trust Christ’s finished work rather than your performance, and show mercy to others because you have received mercy (Matthew 5:7).

question: Who is the head of the church, biblically speaking?
answer:
Biblically speaking, **Jesus Christ is the head of the church**. He is not merely its founder or most honored teacher, but its living Lord and supreme authority.

- **Ephesians 1:22–23:** “And God put everything under His feet and made Him head over everything for the church, which is His body, the fullness of Him who fills everything in every way.”
- **Colossians 1:18:** “And He is the head of the body, the church. He is the beginning and firstborn from among the dead, so that in everything He may be preeminent.”
- **Ephesians 5:23:** “For the husband is the head of the wife as Christ is the head of the church, His body, of which He is the Savior.”

The church is therefore **Christ’s body**, purchased by His blood, governed by His Word, and sustained by His Spirit. Pastors and elders exercise real authority, but only as servants under Christ, the Chief Shepherd, never as replacements for Him. **1 Peter 5:2–4**; **1 Timothy 3:1–7**.

This truth is often summarized by the term **Christ’s headship**: Christ alone is the church’s supreme Lord and mediator. Because He is the head, the church must submit to Scripture and continually direct worship, doctrine, and mission toward Him.

question: Who is the ancient serpent of Revelation 12:9?
answer:
The “ancient serpent” in Revelation 12:9 is **the devil, Satan**, the personal spiritual enemy of God and His people. The verse identifies him by four names:

> “And the great dragon was hurled down, that ancient serpent called the devil and Satan, the deceiver of the whole world. He was hurled to the earth, and his angels with him.”  
> **Revelation 12:9 BSB**

“Ancient serpent” connects Satan with the serpent who deceived Eve in Eden, though Genesis first calls him “the serpent” and Revelation gives the inspired identification. His character is consistent throughout Scripture: he deceives, accuses, tempts, and opposes God’s people. Compare **Genesis 3:1–15; John 8:44; 2 Corinthians 11:3; 1 Peter 5:8**.

The name **Satan** means adversary, while **devil** refers to a slanderer or false accuser. Revelation 12 also announces that he is ultimately defeated through Christ’s saving work: “the accuser of our brothers has been thrown down” because of “the blood of the Lamb” (**Revelation 12:10–11 BSB**). Christians therefore take spiritual opposition seriously, but not fearfully, because Christ has decisively conquered sin, death, and the devil through His death and bodily resurrection.

question: Book of 1 John - Bible Survey
answer:
# Survey of 1 John

**1 John** is a pastoral letter written by the apostle John to strengthen believers in true Christian faith, fellowship with God, assurance of salvation, and holy living. John writes with the authority of an eyewitness of Jesus Christ and directly opposes false teachers who denied that Jesus Christ truly came in the flesh.

## Author and Setting

The letter does not name its author, but its language, theology, and close relationship to the Gospel of John strongly identify the writer as **John the apostle**, one of the Twelve and an eyewitness of Jesus’ earthly ministry. John likely wrote from or near **Ephesus** to churches in Asia Minor toward the end of the first century.

The false teaching John confronts appears to have denied essential truths about Jesus’ incarnation and perhaps claimed spiritual knowledge while treating sin lightly. John does not treat these errors as harmless differences because they distort the identity of Christ and the nature of salvation.

## Purpose

John gives several purposes for writing:

- **To establish fellowship with God and His people:** “We proclaim to you what we have seen and heard, so that you also may have fellowship with us” (1 John 1:3).
- **To promote joy:** “We are writing these things so that our joy may be complete” (1 John 1:4).
- **To call believers away from sin:** “I am writing these things to you so that you will not sin” (1 John 2:1).
- **To warn against false teachers:** 1 John 2:18–27; 1 John 4:1–6.
- **To give assurance of eternal life:** “I have written these things to you who believe in the name of the Son of God, so that you may know that you have eternal life” (1 John 5:13).

## Major Themes

### 1. The Reality of Jesus Christ

John begins by emphasizing that Jesus was physically and historically real:

> “What was from the beginning, what we have heard, what we have seen with our eyes, what we have observed and touched with our hands” (1 John 1:1).

Jesus is not merely a spiritual appearance or an enlightened teacher. He is the eternal Son who truly became man. This is the biblical foundation for the doctrine of the **Incarnation** and the **hypostatic union**, meaning Jesus Christ is one Person with a truly divine nature and a truly human nature.

John also states plainly:

> “Every spirit that confesses that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh is from God” (1 John 4:2).

### 2. Fellowship with God Requires Walking in the Light

God is holy and sin cannot be treated casually:

> “God is Light, and in Him there is no darkness at all” (1 John 1:5).

To “walk in the light” means to live openly before God in faith, truth, repentance, and obedience. Christians are not sinless in this life, but they do not make peace with sin. When believers confess their sins, God is faithful to forgive and cleanse them through Christ’s atoning work (1 John 1:7–2:2).

John presents both the seriousness of sin and the sufficiency of Christ:

> “If anyone does sin, we have an advocate before the Father, Jesus Christ, the Righteous One. He Himself is the atoning sacrifice for our sins” (1 John 2:1–2).

This reflects **penal substitutionary atonement**: Christ died as the righteous substitute for sinners, satisfying divine justice and reconciling His people to God.

### 3. Obedience as Evidence of Genuine Faith

John does not teach salvation by works. Rather, obedience is evidence that a person truly knows Christ:

> “By this we can be sure that we have come to know Him: if we keep His commandments” (1 John 2:3).

Justification is by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone, but genuine faith produces progressive **sanctification**. A person may stumble, yet the settled direction of Christian life is toward obedience rather than rebellion.

### 4. Love for Fellow Believers

Love for Christians is another mark of spiritual life:

> “Anyone who does not love remains in death” (1 John 3:14).

Christian love is not merely affection or sentiment. It reflects the self-giving love of Christ and expresses itself in practical care for brothers and sisters in need (1 John 3:16–18). Love for God and love for His people belong together.

### 5. Testing the Spirits

John commands believers to exercise discernment:

> “Beloved, do not believe every spirit, but test the spirits to see whether they are from God” (1 John 4:1).

The central test concerns Jesus Christ. Any teaching that denies His true incarnation and apostolic Gospel is not from God. John also teaches that believers must distinguish between the Spirit of truth and the spirit of error (1 John 4:6). Christian love does not require accepting false doctrine.

### 6. Assurance of Salvation

The letter repeatedly gives tests by which believers may examine their lives:

- Do I confess the true Jesus Christ? (1 John 4:2–3)
- Do I trust in Christ rather than reject Him?
- Do I desire obedience to God? (1 John 2:3–6)
- Do I love fellow believers? (1 John 3:14–18)
- Do I continue in the apostolic Gospel? (1 John 2:24–27)
- Do I recognize sin and confess it rather than justify it? (1 John 1:8–10)

These are not grounds for boasting or earning salvation. They are evidences of God’s saving work. John’s goal is that believers may **know** they have eternal life, not live in continual uncertainty (1 John 5:13).

## Outline of 1 John

1. **The Word of Life and Fellowship with God**  
   1 John 1:1–4

2. **Walking in the Light**  
   1 John 1:5–2:2

3. **Obedience, Love, and Separation from the World**  
   1 John 2:3–27

4. **God’s Children and the Practice of Righteousness**  
   1 John 2:28–3:24

5. **Testing Spirits and Abiding in God’s Love**  
   1 John 4:1–21

6. **Faith in Christ, Victory, Assurance, and Avoiding Idols**  
   1 John 5:1–21

## Key Verses

> “I have written these things to you who believe in the name of the Son of God, so that you may know that you have eternal life” (1 John 5:13).

> “We love because He first loved us” (1 John 4:19).

> “The one who has the Son has life; the one who does not have the Son of God does not have life” (1 John 5:12).

## Practical Significance

First John teaches that assurance rests neither on sinless perfection nor on empty profession. The Christian looks to Christ’s finished atonement and also sees the confirming fruit of faith: confession of sin, obedience, love, perseverance, and confession of the true Christ.

A helpful way to study this letter is to read it slowly while marking repeated words such as **know, love, abide, truth, life, witness, and sin**. Then ask God to expose false confidence, strengthen genuine assurance, and produce in you the obedience and love that flow from union with Christ.

question: What happens at the final judgment?
answer:
At the final judgment, Jesus Christ will return bodily and visibly, raise the dead, and judge every person with perfect righteousness. “The dead, great and small, standing before the throne” will be judged according to their deeds, and everyone whose name is not found in the Book of Life will face the second death, the lake of fire (Revelation 20:11–15; Acts 17:31).

Several truths stand out:

- **Christ is the Judge.** God has appointed Jesus to judge the living and the dead, so the judgment will be perfectly wise, holy, and impartial (John 5:22–30; 2 Corinthians 5:10).
- **All people will appear before Him.** No one will be exempt, and hidden words, motives, and deeds will be brought to light (Romans 2:5–8; Ecclesiastes 12:14; Matthew 12:36).
- **Works will be judged as evidence.** Scripture does not teach that anyone earns salvation by works. Rather, works reveal the reality of a person’s faith and allegiance. Those justified by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone will be publicly vindicated, while persistent unbelief and sin will be exposed (Matthew 25:31–46; Ephesians 2:8–10; James 2:17–18).
- **Believers will not be condemned.** Whoever trusts in Christ has already passed from death to life and will not come under condemnation (John 5:24; Romans 8:1). Christ’s penal substitution, His death bearing the judgment deserved by His people, is the believer’s only hope.
- **The wicked will face everlasting punishment.** The final judgment is not merely correction or temporary suffering, but righteous and irreversible condemnation apart from God’s saving mercy (Matthew 25:46; 2 Thessalonians 1:8–9).
- **God will renew all things.** After judgment, God will bring His redeemed people into the new heavens and new earth, where righteousness dwells and death, mourning, and pain are no more (2 Peter 3:13; Revelation 21:1–5).

The final judgment will therefore display both God’s justice and His mercy. No one will be condemned unfairly, and no one will be saved by personal merit. Salvation is found only in Jesus Christ, who died for sinners, was buried, rose bodily on the third day, and now reigns as Lord (Acts 4:12; 1 Timothy 2:5–6).

Turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose for forgiveness and eternal life. What aspect of the final judgment most concerns or interests you?

question: In what ways is becoming a Christian becoming an entirely new man / woman?
answer:
Becoming a Christian means that God makes you **a new creation in Christ**, not merely a morally improved version of your old self. The Bible calls this **regeneration**, the Holy Spirit’s giving of spiritual life, and it begins a lifelong work of **sanctification**, becoming increasingly like Jesus.

> “Therefore if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation. The old has passed away. Behold, the new has come!”  
> 2 Corinthians 5:17

This newness appears in several ways:

- **A new standing before God.** You are no longer condemned, but justified, declared righteous through faith in Christ rather than through your works. “Therefore, since we have been justified through faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ” (Romans 5:1).

- **A new heart and spiritual life.** You were spiritually dead in sin, but God makes you alive with Christ. The new birth gives you new affections, so you begin to love God, His Word, holiness, and His people. Ephesians 2:4–5; 1 Peter 1:23.

- **A new Lord.** You no longer belong to yourself. Jesus Christ, who died and rose bodily, becomes your rightful Lord and Savior. “He died for all, that those who live should no longer live for themselves, but for Him who died for them and was raised again” (2 Corinthians 5:15).

- **A new relationship to sin.** Christians are not instantly sinless, but they are no longer content to make peace with sin. The Holy Spirit produces repentance and a growing desire for obedience. Sin may still wound you, but it is no longer your rightful master. Romans 6:6–14; Galatians 5:16–17.

- **A new identity and belonging.** You become adopted by God, united to Christ, and made part of His people. You are not defined ultimately by your past, failures, achievements, or other human labels, but by belonging to Christ. Galatians 2:20; Romans 8:15–17; 1 Peter 2:9–10.

- **A new purpose.** Your life is redirected toward knowing God, loving your neighbor, serving the church, and proclaiming Christ. “We are God’s workmanship, created in Christ Jesus to do good works” (Ephesians 2:10).

- **A new hope.** God will not abandon the work He has begun. The Christian’s renewal is presently partial, but it will be completed when Christ returns and transforms His people fully. Philippians 1:6; 1 John 3:2–3.

This does not mean your personality, memories, vocation, or earthly relationships are erased. Rather, God redeems you as the person He created you to be, cleansing your guilt and reshaping every part of your life under Christ’s lordship. The “old man” or “old woman” refers to your former identity and dominion in Adam, while the “new man” or “new woman” is the renewed life of those united to Christ (Ephesians 4:22–24; Colossians 3:9–11).

The foundation is not self-reformation. God is holy, and our sin separates us from Him, so we need a Savior. Jesus Christ became truly man while remaining truly God, lived without sin, died on the cross as the substitute for sinners, was buried, and rose bodily on the third day. Salvation is by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone, not by becoming good enough. Turn from your sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone for forgiveness, righteousness, and new life.

A practical next step is to read Ephesians 1–4 slowly, asking God to show you both what is already true of you in Christ and what must increasingly change in your daily life.

question: What are the Pauline epistles?
answer:
The **Pauline epistles** are the letters in the New Testament traditionally written by the apostle Paul to churches and individual Christians. They teach the gospel of Jesus Christ, explain Christian doctrine, correct error, and give practical instruction for godly living.

The **thirteen letters traditionally attributed to Paul** are:

1. Romans  
2. 1 Corinthians  
3. 2 Corinthians  
4. Galatians  
5. Ephesians  
6. Philippians  
7. Colossians  
8. 1 Thessalonians  
9. 2 Thessalonians  
10. 1 Timothy  
11. 2 Timothy  
12. Titus  
13. Philemon  

**Hebrews** has sometimes been associated with Paul historically, but its author is not identified in the letter, so it is usually treated separately from the Pauline epistles.

Paul’s letters emphasize truths such as **justification by faith**, union with Christ, the work of the Holy Spirit, the holiness of the church, and Christian perseverance. At the center is the historical gospel: Christ died for our sins, was buried, and was raised bodily on the third day, according to the Scriptures (1 Corinthians 15:3–4).

question: How can I be sure I am praying according to the will of God?
answer:
You can be sure you are praying according to God’s will when your requests agree with Scripture, seek God’s glory, and are offered with a submissive heart rather than a demand that God fulfill your preferred outcome.

The clearest promise is:

> “And this is the confidence that we have before Him: If we ask anything according to His will, He hears us. And if we know that He hears us, we know that we have what we have asked of Him.”  
> **1 John 5:14–15**

Several biblical guides can help:

- **Pray according to God’s revealed Word.** God will not lead you to ask for what He has forbidden or contradict what He has commanded. Jesus taught His disciples to pray, “Your kingdom come, Your will be done, on earth as it is in heaven” (**Matthew 6:10**).
- **Ask for what honors God, not merely what satisfies self.** Sinful motives can distort prayer: “You ask and do not receive because you ask with wrong motives, that you may squander it on your pleasures” (**James 4:3**).
- **Bring your desires honestly, then surrender them trustingly.** Jesus Himself prayed in Gethsemane, “Yet not My will, but Yours be done” (**Luke 22:42**). Submission is not unbelief. It is faith in God’s wisdom, goodness, and sovereignty.
- **Pray through Christ.** Because Jesus is the one mediator between God and sinners, Christians approach the Father through His finished work, not through their own merit (**1 Timothy 2:5–6; Hebrews 4:14–16**).
- **Seek wisdom and godly counsel.** God ordinarily guides His people through Scripture, prayer, wise counsel, and providential circumstances, while Scripture remains the final authority: “Trust in the LORD with all your heart, and lean not on your own understanding” (**Proverbs 3:5–6**).
- **Remember that uncertainty does not mean your prayer failed.** The Holy Spirit helps us when we do not know what to pray, interceding for us according to God’s will (**Romans 8:26–27**).

A practical pattern is to ask: **Is this request biblical? Does it seek God’s glory and another’s good? Am I willing to receive either “yes,” “no,” or “wait”?** Then pray specifically, search the relevant Scriptures, and discuss the matter with a mature believer or church elder. God’s will is not discovered by chasing impressions, but by walking faithfully in the light He has already given. Take time today to pray through **Matthew 6:9–13**, slowly turning each phrase into your own request.

question: What does the Bible say about busyness / being too busy?
answer:
The Bible does not condemn **diligence**, but it warns against a life so crowded that we neglect God, love, wisdom, and the responsibilities He has actually given us. Busyness can become sinful when it is driven by anxiety, pride, greed, people-pleasing, or a refusal to rest and receive our limits.

Jesus corrected Martha, not because serving was wrong, but because anxious distraction had displaced fellowship with Him:

> “Martha, Martha,” the Lord replied, “you are worried and upset about many things. But only one thing is necessary. Mary has chosen the better part, and it will not be taken away from her.”  
> **Luke 10:41–42**

Several biblical principles help us:

- **Put communion with Christ first.** Jesus Himself withdrew from crowds to pray: **Mark 1:35**; **Luke 5:15–16**. A full schedule is no substitute for abiding in Christ, which is central to sanctification.
- **Do not confuse constant activity with faithfulness.** Scripture calls us to “walk circumspectly,” making wise use of time, not merely filling every moment: **Ephesians 5:15–17**.
- **Receive God’s gift of rest.** God established a pattern of work and rest, and Jesus told His disciples, “Come with Me privately to a secluded place and rest a while” (**Mark 6:31**). Rest is not laziness when it helps us serve God and neighbor faithfully.
- **Reject anxious striving.** “Be still and know that I am God” (**Psalm 46:10**), and “Cast all your anxiety on Him, because He cares for you” (**1 Peter 5:7**). Busyness often becomes an attempt to control what belongs in God’s hands.
- **Practice responsible diligence.** The answer is not passivity. Believers should work faithfully, care for their households, serve others, and avoid idleness: **Colossians 3:23–24**; **2 Thessalonians 3:10–12**.
- **Know that your worth is not measured by productivity.** Your acceptance before God rests on grace and justification by faith in Christ, not on how much you accomplish: **Ephesians 2:8–10**; **Romans 5:1**.

A helpful question is not merely, “How can I fit more into my day?” but, **“What has God actually called me to do in this season, and what am I doing from fear or vanity?”** This week, set aside a quiet period to pray through **Psalm 90:12**, review your commitments, remove one unnecessary obligation, and protect regular time for Scripture, prayer, worship, sleep, and meaningful fellowship.

question: What are the seven baptisms mentioned in the Bible, and what do they mean?
answer:
The Bible does not present a formal list titled “the seven baptisms.” However, Christians commonly identify seven distinct uses of the word **baptism** in Scripture. They are not all the same kind of baptism, and some are descriptive rather than commands for the church.

1. **The baptism of Moses**

Israel was “baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea,” when God brought them through the Red Sea under Moses’ leadership.

**1 Corinthians 10:1–2**

This was a historical and typological identification with Moses and the covenant community. It points forward to salvation through God’s appointed Redeemer, though it did not mean that every Israelite possessed saving faith.

2. **John’s baptism**

John baptized people in water as a sign of repentance and preparation for the coming Messiah.

**Mark 1:4–5; Matthew 3:1–6**

John’s baptism was preparatory and belonged to the transition from the old covenant era to Christ’s revealed ministry. It was not identical to Christian baptism. In Ephesus, people who had received only John’s baptism were baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus after hearing the fuller gospel.

**Acts 19:1–5**

3. **Jesus’ baptism of suffering**

Jesus spoke of His approaching suffering and death as a “baptism” that He must undergo.

**Mark 10:38–39; Luke 12:50**

This refers figuratively to Christ being overwhelmed by the suffering, judgment-bearing, and death He willingly endured for His people. It is closely connected with **penal substitution**, the truth that Christ bore the judgment due to sinners on the cross.

4. **Baptism in the Holy Spirit**

All who truly belong to Christ are baptized by one Spirit into His one body.

**1 Corinthians 12:13**

This describes the Spirit’s work of uniting believers to Christ and His church. It is not a second class of Christian, but part of conversion and union with Christ. The Spirit applies Christ’s saving work to believers.

5. **Baptism with fire**

John said that Jesus would baptize with the Holy Spirit and fire.

**Matthew 3:11–12; Luke 3:16–17**

The immediate context speaks of judgment, separating wheat from chaff and burning the chaff with unquenchable fire. Therefore, this primarily refers to Christ’s eschatological judgment on the wicked, not merely to an emotional or intensified Christian experience. The imagery of fire at Pentecost is related, but the context in Matthew and Luke emphasizes judgment.

6. **Christian baptism in water**

Jesus commanded His disciples to baptize those who become His followers in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.

**Matthew 28:18–20; Acts 2:38–41; Romans 6:3–4**

This is the church’s ordinance, an outward sign of repentance and faith in Christ, union with Him in His death and resurrection, and entrance into the visible church. Baptism does not justify a sinner. **Justification is by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone**, not by the act of baptism, as seen in passages such as **Ephesians 2:8–9** and **Romans 3:28**. Christians should therefore be baptized in obedience to Christ, but they must not trust baptism instead of Christ.

7. **“Baptism for the dead”**

Paul mentions people who were being baptized “for the dead.”

**1 Corinthians 15:29**

This is one of the most difficult verses in the New Testament. Paul refers to a practice known to the Corinthians, but he does not command or clearly approve proxy baptism for deceased people. The surrounding argument concerns the certainty of bodily resurrection, and Paul’s point is that such a practice would be pointless if the dead are not raised. Scripture consistently presents a person’s response to God as occurring during life, and it gives no command or example for baptizing someone on behalf of the dead.

The ordinary Christian baptism that Christ commands is therefore **believer’s baptism in water**, practiced as a sign of genuine repentance and faith. At the same time, **Ephesians 4:5** speaks of “one Lord, one faith, one baptism,” referring to the unity of Christ’s people in the one Christian baptism, rather than denying that Scripture uses the word “baptism” in several different ways.

question: What do you think about the Bible codes? Is there any validity to them?
answer:
“Bible codes” usually refer to alleged hidden messages found by skipping equal numbers of letters in the Hebrew text, often called **equidistant letter sequences**. While patterns can certainly be found in biblical texts, there is no reliable evidence that these patterns convey a supernatural prediction system or an intended secret code.

The main problems are:

- **Any long text can produce striking patterns** when researchers choose the spacing, starting point, spelling, and word forms after looking at the results.
- The Hebrew Bible has a large number of letters, so many apparent “discoveries” can arise by chance.
- Different Hebrew manuscripts, vowel markings, spelling conventions, and translation traditions can affect the results.
- Attempts to test the method under controlled conditions have not established that it predicts events better than chance.

That does not mean the Bible is merely an ordinary book. Christians believe it is the inspired, inerrant Word of God, but its divine authority does not depend on concealed mathematical messages. Scripture presents itself as God’s revealed Word meant to be read, understood, proclaimed, and obeyed: “Your word is a lamp to my feet and a light to my path” (Psalm 119:105).
