You may still remember what happened, but God does not hold forgiven sin against you as a debt. In Christ, you are not required to redeem yourself. Christ has redeemed His people.

**4. Learn what the regret is meant to teach you, then press forward.**  
Paul did not pretend that his former life had never happened, but he refused to remain imprisoned by it:

> “Forgetting what is behind and straining toward what is ahead, I press on toward the goal to win the prize of God’s heavenly calling in Christ Jesus.”  
> **Philippians 3:13–14**

“Forget” here does not mean erasing memory. It means refusing to live as though the past has greater authority than Christ’s grace and present calling. Ask, “What should I learn, confess, repair, or change?” Then walk forward in obedience.

**5. Remember God’s providence without calling evil good.**  
The Bible never says that sin was harmless. Yet God is able to work even through painful failures and losses:

> “We know that God works all things together for the good of those who love Him, who are called according to His purpose.”  
> **Romans 8:28**

Joseph could say to those who had harmed him, “You intended to harm me, but God intended it for good” (**Genesis 50:20**). God’s providence does not excuse wrongdoing, but it means your past is not stronger than His purposes.

A practical path may be: confess the matter to God, speak with a mature pastor or trusted believer, make restitution where Scripture requires it, write down the specific truth of God’s forgiveness, and meditate daily on **Psalm 51**, **Romans 8:1**, and **Philippians 3:13–14**. If the regret is overwhelming or connected to trauma, seek help from your pastor and a qualified biblical counselor.

If you have never trusted Christ, do not try to cleanse your conscience by regret or good works. Turn from your sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose for forgiveness and new life. What regret is weighing on you most heavily right now?

question: Monergism vs. synergism - which view is correct?
answer:
In the question of **conversion and justification**, monergism is correct: God alone effectually accomplishes salvation, giving life to spiritually dead sinners, while the sinner truly repents and believes as the result of God’s grace, not as a contribution that earns salvation.

The best case for historic synergism, especially Arminian or Wesleyan theology, is that Scripture repeatedly commands all people to repent and believe, speaks of resisting the Holy Spirit, and presents faith as the necessary human response, for example, Acts 7:51; John 3:16; Revelation 22:17.

Yet the Bible teaches that fallen humanity is not merely weak but spiritually dead and unable to submit to God apart from divine grace: “There is no one who understands, no one who seeks God” (Romans 3:11); “you were dead in your trespasses and sins” (Ephesians 2:1); and “no one can come to Me unless the Father who sent Me draws him” (John 6:44). God’s saving work begins with His gracious choice, regenerating call, and effective work: “It does not, therefore, depend on man’s desire or effort, but on God’s mercy” (Romans 9:16); “Even when we were dead in our trespasses, made us alive with Christ” (Ephesians 2:5); “Those God foreknew He also predestined... called... justified... and glorified” (Romans 8:29–30).

So I affirm **monergism in regeneration and justification**, often called the doctrines of effectual calling and justification by faith alone. Faith is indispensable, but it is the empty hand receiving Christ, not a meritorious work or autonomous contribution. Salvation is “by grace you have been saved through faith... it is the gift of God, not by works” (Ephesians 2:8–9). This does not make repentance and faith unreal or unnecessary. God commands them, and the person genuinely responds, but God’s grace makes that response possible and certain.

The crucial distinction is this: **monergism does not mean God saves people apart from faith; it means God sovereignly gives the grace by which His people willingly come to faith**. As Jesus said, “All that the Father gives Me will come to Me” (John 6:37).

In sanctification, Christians truly cooperate with God through obedience, prayer, and the means of grace, while still confessing that God is the One working in them: “It is God who works in you to will and to act on behalf of His good purpose” (Philippians 2:13). Therefore, synergistic language can describe the believer’s response in sanctification, but **monergism best describes the origin and accomplishment of salvation**.

question: Did Old Testament believers have eternal security?
answer:
Yes. Old Testament believers who truly trusted God were eternally secure, not because of their works or because they perfectly kept the law, but because God justified them by grace through faith and secured their salvation through the promised work of Christ.

Abraham is the clearest example: “Abram believed the LORD, and it was credited to him as righteousness” (Genesis 15:6; Romans 4:1–8). David likewise spoke of the blessedness of the person whose sins God forgives, apart from works (Psalm 32:1–2; Romans 4:6–8). Their justification rested on Christ’s future atonement, even though they looked forward to it by faith. Hebrews says that Christ’s death redeemed those under the first covenant (Hebrews 9:15).

The Old Testament believers were saved by the same gospel as New Testament believers, though with less complete revelation:

- They trusted God’s promise of redemption, while Christians look back to Christ’s completed work (Genesis 3:15; Hebrews 11:13; 1 Peter 1:10–12).
- They were justified by faith, not by law-keeping (Habakkuk 2:4; Romans 4:9–12).
- God preserved them to the end, because salvation depends on His faithfulness, not human strength (Psalm 37:23–24; Psalm 138:8; Philippians 1:6).
- Their eternal life was secured by the same Christ who is “the mediator of a new covenant” (Hebrews 9:15).

This does not mean every physical descendant of Abraham was spiritually saved. Scripture distinguishes outward membership in Israel from true faith: “Not all who are descended from Israel are Israel” (Romans 9:6). The true people of God in every age are those who trust His promise, and those whom God truly saves He keeps. Jesus said, “No one can snatch them out of My hand” (John 10:28), and that promise applies to God’s redeemed people, including the saints who lived before the cross.

So, yes, Old Testament believers had eternal security, although their assurance was often less fully informed than ours. Their security was grounded in God’s covenant faithfulness and ultimately in the penal substitutionary sacrifice of Jesus Christ.

question: What does it mean that the church is the bride of Christ?
answer:
The church is called **the bride of Christ** because Jesus has entered into a covenant relationship with His redeemed people, loving, cleansing, protecting, and preparing them for eternal union with Him. The image emphasizes Christ’s faithful love and the church’s joyful, exclusive devotion to Him.

Paul explains this through marriage:

> “Husbands, love your wives, just as Christ loved the church and gave Himself up for her to sanctify her, cleansing her by the washing with water through the word, and to present her to Himself as a glorious church, without stain or wrinkle or any such blemish, but holy and blameless.”  
> **Ephesians 5:25–27**

Several truths are pictured:

- **Christ’s sacrificial love:** Jesus gave Himself for the church. This is **penal substitutionary atonement**, the truth that Christ bore sin’s judgment in the place of His people so they could be reconciled to God.
- **The church’s sanctification:** Christ is actively making His people holy through His Word and Spirit. The bride is not accepted because she is already perfect, but because Christ redeems and purifies her.
- **Covenant faithfulness:** As a bride is devoted to her husband, the church belongs exclusively to Christ and must not give its worship to idols or false saviors. Paul describes the church as being betrothed to Christ and urges faithful devotion to Him, **2 Corinthians 11:2–3**.
- **Future hope:** The image points toward Christ’s return, when the church will be presented to Him in glory at “the marriage supper of the Lamb,” **Revelation 19:6–9**. The final vision of Scripture speaks of the holy city as “the bride, the wife of the Lamb,” **Revelation 21:9–10**.

This does not mean the church is divine or that believers become part of God’s essence. Rather, it is a covenant metaphor expressing communion, love, holiness, belonging, and eternal fellowship with the true Bridegroom, Jesus Christ.

Practically, Christians should treat the church with both love and seriousness: Christ gave Himself for her, so we should pursue unity, holiness, mutual care, and faithfulness to His Word. The church’s hope is not that she will make herself worthy, but that Christ will faithfully complete the sanctifying work He began, **Philippians 1:6**.

question: How can I believe in the goodness of God when there is so much evil in the world?
answer:
Your question is not shallow or faithless. Evil can make God’s goodness feel difficult to trust, especially when suffering is personal, prolonged, or apparently unanswered. Christians do not believe evil is imaginary, insignificant, or outside God’s notice.

The Bible gives several truths that hold together:

- **God is good and holy.** Evil is not something God calls good or takes pleasure in. “God is light, and in Him there is no darkness at all” (1 John 1:5). He is patient and merciful, yet His wrath against sin is real (Psalm 5:4; Romans 2:4–6).
- **Humanity’s rebellion brought sin and death into God’s good creation.** The world is not as God originally made it. Scripture describes creation as subjected to frustration and groaning because of sin (Genesis 3:16–19; Romans 8:20–23). This does not explain every particular tragedy, and Jesus warns us not to assume that every victim suffered because of some unusually wicked personal sin (Luke 13:1–5; John 9:1–3).
- **God is not distant from suffering.** In the incarnation, the eternal Son truly became man. Jesus was rejected, betrayed, abused, crucified, and buried. At the cross, God did not offer an abstract explanation of suffering. He entered it Himself. Christ’s death was **penal substitution**, bearing the judgment sinners deserve, and His bodily resurrection showed that sin and death will not have the final word (Isaiah 53:4–6; Acts 2:23–24; 1 Peter 2:24).
- **God will judge evil perfectly.** Much injustice remains hidden from human courts, but none is hidden from God. Jesus Christ will return bodily to judge the living and the dead, and God will renew creation so that “there will be no more death or mourning or crying or pain” (Ecclesiastes 12:14; Acts 17:31; Revelation 21:1–5).

This does not mean we can explain why God permits every particular evil. Scripture gives us something stronger than a complete explanation: God’s character, His presence with sufferers, His promise to redeem, and His commitment to judge. The cross assures us that God’s goodness is not sentimental. He is so opposed to evil that He dealt with it at the cost of His beloved Son, and so merciful that He offers forgiveness to sinners.

There is also an important personal matter. The world’s evil is not only “out there” in other people. Scripture says that all have sinned and fall short of God’s glory (Romans 3:23). We need more than better circumstances. We need a Savior. God sent Jesus Christ, truly God and truly man, who lived without sin, died on the cross for sinners, was buried, and rose bodily on the third day. Salvation is by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone, not by works (Ephesians 2:8–9).

Turn from your sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose again to forgive sinners and give new life. As you wrestle with this, read Psalm 73 slowly and bring your honest questions directly to God, while also speaking with a mature pastor or trusted Christian who can walk with you. What kind of evil or suffering has most strongly challenged your trust in God’s goodness?

question: What does "communion of the saints" mean in the ancient creeds?
answer:
The **“communion of the saints”** means the spiritual fellowship and shared life of all who belong to Jesus Christ, united to Him and therefore united to one another. In the Apostles’ Creed, “saints” means God’s holy people, not merely a special class of unusually mature Christians.

The phrase likely includes two closely related ideas:

- **Communion among holy people:** Christians share one faith, one Lord, one Spirit, and one spiritual family. “There is one body and one Spirit” (Ephesians 4:4–6). Believers are members of one another and are called to bear one another’s burdens (Romans 12:4–5; Galatians 6:2).
- **Participation in holy things:** Christians share in the blessings of Christ, especially through the preaching of the Word, prayer, and the Lord’s Supper. “The cup of blessing that we bless, is it not a participation in the blood of Christ?” (1 Corinthians 10:16–17).

This communion extends beyond one congregation and across time. All who are united to Christ belong to His one Church, including believers who have died and are now with the Lord, though Scripture directs our worship and prayers to God, not to departed believers. The living Church is encouraged by the example of those who have gone before us (Hebrews 12:1), while Christ alone is the mediator between God and humanity (1 Timothy 2:5).

The doctrine therefore teaches that Christianity is not an isolated relationship with God. Those justified by faith in Christ are adopted into God’s household, progressively sanctified together, and called to worship, serve, correct, comfort, and encourage one another. A concrete application is to commit yourself to a faithful local church, where this communion is practiced through Word, prayer, fellowship, and the Lord’s Supper.

question: How can I gain a passion for winning souls?
answer:
A passion for winning souls grows as you know Christ more deeply, love people more sincerely, and remember the eternal weight of the gospel. It cannot be manufactured by emotional pressure; it is cultivated by the Holy Spirit through Scripture, prayer, and faithful obedience.

Begin with the glory of God. Evangelism is not mainly about becoming impressive or increasing numbers. It is about seeing people reconciled to their holy Creator through Jesus Christ. Paul said, “The love of Christ compels us” (2 Corinthians 5:14), and Jesus was moved with compassion when He saw the crowds “harassed and helpless, like sheep without a shepherd” (Matthew 9:36).

Keep the gospel clear in your own heart. We are sinners separated from God and unable to save ourselves. Jesus Christ, truly God and truly man, lived righteously, died as the substitute for sinners, was buried, and rose bodily on the third day. Salvation is by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone, not by our works (Ephesians 2:8–9; 1 Corinthians 15:3–4). The more freshly you treasure that grace, the more naturally you will speak of it.

Pray specifically, not merely for “boldness,” but for particular people by name. Ask God to open their hearts, give you opportunities, and make you attentive to their spiritual and personal needs. Paul asked believers to pray “that God may open to us a door for the word” (Colossians 4:3–4). You might pray through a short list each morning and ask God for one opportunity to speak or serve someone that day.

Also remember that God alone gives new birth. Your responsibility is faithful witness, not conversion. “I planted the seed and Apollos watered it, but God made it grow” (1 Corinthians 3:6). This frees you from both pride when someone responds and despair when someone refuses. Speak truthfully, listen patiently, and leave the results with the Lord.

A simple pattern for growth could be:

- Read one Gospel passage daily, asking, “What does this show me about Jesus?”
- Pray for three unbelieving people by name.
- Prepare a two-minute testimony of your sin, Christ’s mercy, and how you came to trust Him.
- Share the gospel with one person each week, naturally and respectfully.
- Serve alongside mature believers who regularly evangelize.
- Invite people not merely to church activities, but to repent and trust in Jesus Christ.

Do not wait until you feel great passion before obeying. Often passion follows obedience. As you lovingly speak the truth, God may enlarge your compassion and give you “a heart of wisdom” regarding the brevity of life (Psalm 90:12). Ask Him to make you faithful, not frantic, and courageous, not combative.

This week, choose three names, pray for them daily, and look for one humble opportunity to ask about their beliefs or share what Christ has done for you. Is your main difficulty fear of rejection, uncertainty about what to say, or lack of compassion for those who are lost?

question: What is reprobation? What does it mean to be reprobate?
answer:
**Reprobation** is the theological term for God’s righteous decision to pass over some sinners, leaving them in their sin and ordaining their just condemnation, while saving others by His grace. In Reformed theology, reprobation is understood alongside election, but it is not symmetrical: God gives mercy to the elect, while the reprobate are condemned for their own willing and culpable sin, not for innocent unbelief.

Scripture teaches both God’s sovereign authority and human responsibility:

- **Romans 9:18–23** speaks of God showing mercy to whom He wills and enduring “vessels of wrath” prepared for destruction.
- **Romans 1:24, 26, 28** describes God giving persistent sinners over to the desires and consequences of their rebellion.
- **2 Thessalonians 2:10–12** says that those who refuse the truth and delight in wickedness are judged.
- **Ezekiel 18:23** shows that God takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked, but calls them to turn and live.

To be **reprobate** means to be rejected, morally corrupt, or disqualified. The New Testament uses this language in several ways:

- In **Romans 1:28**, the phrase “depraved mind” describes people who persistently reject God and are given over to sinful thinking.
- In **Titus 1:16**, people may profess to know God while denying Him by their actions, being “detestable, disobedient, and unfit for any good deed.”
- In **2 Corinthians 13:5**, “reprobate” can mean failing a test or proving oneself genuine, as in the warning to examine whether one is truly in the faith.

A crucial pastoral distinction is this: **“Reprobate” is not a label Christians should casually place on another person.** We cannot see God’s secret decree or know whether someone may yet repent. Paul himself was once a violent persecutor of the church, yet he received mercy through Christ, **1 Timothy 1:13–16**. The proper response to sin is warning, prayer, evangelism, and a call to repentance, not despair or speculation.

Faithful Christians differ here. Reformed theology understands reprobation as God’s sovereign passing over and just condemnation of sinners, while Arminian and Wesleyan theology generally understands condemnation as grounded in foreseen, persistent unbelief rather than an unconditional decree. I hold the Reformed understanding because it best preserves the biblical teaching of God’s sovereign election while affirming that every condemned sinner is judged for real, willing sin.

Yet Scripture does not give this doctrine so that you would wonder, “Am I secretly reprobate?” The Gospel openly calls sinners to Christ: **“Everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved” (Romans 10:13)**. We are saved by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone, because Jesus truly died as the substitute for sinners, was buried, and bodily rose again, **1 Corinthians 15:3–4**. Turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone for forgiveness and new life.

question: What does the Bible say about how to get baptized / how to baptize?
answer:
The Bible commands baptism for those who repent and believe in Jesus Christ, ordinarily by being immersed in water in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. Baptism is an outward sign of union with Christ, not a work that earns forgiveness or justification.

**Who should be baptized?**  
The consistent pattern in the New Testament is that people hear the gospel, repent, believe, and then receive baptism:

- Jesus commanded His disciples to make disciples, baptizing them “in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matthew 28:19).
- Peter called his hearers to repent and be baptized (Acts 2:38).
- Those who received the gospel were baptized (Acts 2:41; Acts 8:12).
- The Ethiopian official believed and was baptized when they came to water (Acts 8:36–39).
- The household of Cornelius received the Holy Spirit and was then baptized, because they had believed (Acts 10:44–48).

Thus, baptism belongs to professing believers. A person should not wait until he or she feels spiritually perfect. The proper preparation is genuine repentance, faith in Christ, and a willingness to follow Him.

**How should baptism be performed?**  
Jesus gave the Trinitarian command: “in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matthew 28:19). Baptism should involve water and be administered under the authority of Christ’s church. Immersion best represents the biblical picture of being buried and raised with Christ, as shown in Romans 6:3–5 and the fact that John baptized where there was “plenty of water” (John 3:23).

**What does baptism mean?**  
Baptism visibly portrays union with Christ in His death, burial, and resurrection (Romans 6:3–5; Colossians 2:12). It is a public confession that the believer has turned from sin and now belongs to Jesus. It does not itself regenerate or justify, because we are saved by grace through faith in Christ, not by works (Ephesians 2:8–9; Titus 3:5).

Some historic Christians baptize infants, arguing from covenant continuity, household baptisms, and the inclusion of children in the covenant community, while still affirming that salvation is by grace alone through faith alone.  

My position is believer’s baptism by immersion, because the New Testament presents baptism after repentance and faith, and immersion most clearly portrays burial and resurrection with Christ; this is a secondary doctrine on which faithful Christians have disagreed, so it should be practiced with conviction and charity.

If you have trusted in Christ and have not yet been baptized, speak with the elders or pastor of a faithful local church, share your testimony of repentance and faith, and ask to be baptized in obedience to Jesus.

question: What is prevenient grace?
answer:
Prevenient grace is the Wesleyan-Arminian teaching that God’s grace “goes before” conversion, graciously awakening and enabling every fallen person to respond freely to the gospel, either by faith or rejection.

Its strongest biblical case appeals to passages such as John 1:9, Titus 2:11, and John 12:32, understood as describing a universal grace that precedes saving faith.

From a Reformed Baptist perspective, I do not affirm prevenient grace as a distinct universal grace that restores the sinner’s ability to choose Christ; Scripture teaches that sinners are spiritually dead and need God’s **effectual calling**, in which the Holy Spirit gives a new heart and brings them to faith, while still affirming God’s genuine common grace toward all people (Ephesians 2:1–5; John 6:44; Romans 8:7–8; Acts 13:48). Salvation is therefore by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone, not through an autonomous human response (Ephesians 2:8–9).

question: What does it mean that Jesus died for our sins?
answer:
When the Bible says that Jesus “died for our sins,” it means that He willingly stood in the place of guilty sinners and bore the judgment our sins deserved, so that everyone who trusts in Him may be forgiven and reconciled to God.

Sin is not merely weakness or failure. It is rebellion against our holy Creator, leaving us guilty and separated from Him. “The wages of sin is death” (Romans 6:23). Because God is just, sin must be judged, but because He is merciful, He provided a substitute.

Jesus, the sinless Son of God who became truly man, offered Himself on the cross. He was not dying for His own sins, because He had none. Instead, “God made Him who knew no sin to be sin on our behalf, so that in Him we might become the righteousness of God” (2 Corinthians 5:21). This is called **penal substitutionary atonement**: Christ bore the penalty, or judgment, due to His people, and His righteousness is counted to those who believe.

His death was also a real act of reconciliation: “Christ also suffered for sins once for all, the righteous for the unrighteous, to bring you to God” (1 Peter 3:18). The Father did not force an unwilling Son. The Father, Son, and Holy Spirit acted together in holy love to save sinners. Jesus said, “No one takes it from Me, but I lay it down of My own accord” (John 10:18).

The cross is not the end of the Gospel. Jesus was truly buried and bodily raised on the third day, just as Scripture teaches (1 Corinthians 15:3–4). His resurrection confirms that His sacrifice was accepted, sin and death were defeated, and those united to Him receive justification and new life.

You cannot be forgiven by trying to become good enough. Salvation is “by grace through faith,” not by works (Ephesians 2:8–9). Turn from your sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose for your forgiveness and new life.

question: What is Calvinism, and is it biblical?
answer:
Calvinism is a biblical-theological system emphasizing God’s sovereign grace in salvation: sinners are spiritually dead in sin, God graciously elects and calls His people, Christ effectively atones for them, the Spirit brings them to faith, and God preserves them to the end. The name comes from John Calvin, but its central doctrines are rooted in Scripture and were held in various forms by Christians before him.

The classic summary is **TULIP**:

- **Total depravity:** Sin affects every part of humanity, leaving us unable to come to God apart from grace. This does not mean people are as evil as possible, but that sin has corrupted the whole person.  
  **Romans 3:10–12; Ephesians 2:1–3; 1 Corinthians 2:14**

- **Unconditional election:** God’s choice to save is grounded in His mercy and purpose, not foreseen human merit or works.  
  **Ephesians 1:3–6; Romans 9:10–16; John 6:37–44**

- **Particular redemption, often called limited atonement:** Christ’s death is sufficient for all, but it effectively secures salvation for those whom God gives Him.  
  **Matthew 1:21; John 10:11, 14–15; Ephesians 5:25**

- **Effectual calling, often called irresistible grace:** When God inwardly calls His elect through the gospel, He graciously overcomes their resistance and brings them willingly to faith.  
  **Ezekiel 36:26–27; John 6:44; Acts 16:14**

- **Perseverance of the saints:** Everyone truly united to Christ will be preserved by God and will persevere in faith to the end.  
  **John 10:27–30; Romans 8:29–39; Philippians 1:6**

Yes, **Calvinism is biblical**, especially in its teaching that salvation is by grace alone, through faith alone, in Christ alone, and that God is sovereign over salvation. Scripture also clearly teaches genuine human responsibility, the universal command to repent and believe, and the sincere proclamation of the gospel to all people: **Acts 17:30; John 3:16; Romans 10:9–13**.

The strongest Arminian objection is that unconditional election and particular redemption seem to conflict with God’s universal saving desire and meaningful human responsibility, passages such as **1 Timothy 2:3–4; 2 Peter 3:9; 1 John 2:2**. The Reformed response is that these texts must be read alongside Scripture’s equally clear teaching about God’s sovereign election, and that divine sovereignty does not cancel human responsibility.

My position is Reformed Baptist: Calvinism best explains the full biblical pattern of God’s sovereign grace and human responsibility, particularly in **Romans 8:28–30; Romans 9; Ephesians 1:3–14; John 6:35–45**. However, Christians who disagree on these secondary questions should not treat one another as outside the faith, provided they confess the essential gospel: sinners are justified by grace alone through faith alone in the crucified and bodily risen Jesus Christ, not by works.

The practical result should not be speculation or pride, but worship, humility, evangelism, assurance, and holiness. God saves sinners completely, and therefore believers can rest in Christ while actively pursuing sanctification through Scripture, prayer, fellowship, and obedience.

question: Who was Ishtar, and is there any connection between Ishtar and Easter?
answer:
Ishtar was a major Mesopotamian goddess worshiped by Akkadian, Babylonian, and Assyrian peoples. She was associated especially with sexual love, fertility, warfare, and royal power, and was closely related to the earlier Sumerian goddess Inanna. Her worship involved myths and rituals that were part of the religious life of the ancient Near East.

There is **no established historical connection between Ishtar and Easter**. The resemblance between the names is superficial. In English, *Easter* probably comes from the Old English name *Ēastre*, associated with a spring month or festival mentioned by the eighth-century Christian writer Bede. However, the Christian feast itself was not derived from Ishtar worship.

The earliest and central Christian name for the celebration is **Pascha**, from the Greek *pascha*, meaning Passover. Jesus’ death occurred at Passover, and His bodily resurrection on the third day is the foundation of the Christian celebration, as recorded in Matthew 28:1–10; 1 Corinthians 15:3–4. Most languages still use forms of *Pascha*, such as *Pâques*, *Pasqua*, and *Pascua*.

So, the careful distinction is:

- **Ishtar**: an ancient Mesopotamian goddess.
- **Easter as an English word**: likely connected to an Anglo-Saxon spring term, though details are limited.
- **Easter as the Christian feast**: the celebration of Jesus Christ’s historical death, burial, and bodily resurrection, rooted in Passover, not Ishtar.

Christians should therefore avoid repeating the claim that “Easter is Ishtar” as though it were established history. Whatever customs or names developed in different cultures, the biblical substance of the feast is Christ’s victory over sin and death. As Paul says, “Christ has indeed been raised from the dead, the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep” (1 Corinthians 15:20).

question: Who are the Alawites, and what do they believe?
answer:
The **Alawites** are a religious and ethnoreligious community concentrated mainly in **western Syria**, with smaller populations in **Turkey and Lebanon**. They were historically called **Nusayris**, after Muhammad ibn Nusayr, a ninth-century figure associated with their origins. They should not be confused with the **Alevis** of Turkey, who are a distinct community, though the names are sometimes conflated.

Alawite beliefs developed within a broad **Shiite Islamic environment**, but they include distinctive teachings and symbolic interpretations that set them apart from both Sunni Islam and mainstream Twelver Shiism. Their tradition has historically been esoteric, meaning that some teachings were reserved for initiated members. Major features commonly associated with Alawite belief include:

- **Strong devotion to Ali ibn Abi Talib**, Muhammad’s cousin and son-in-law, whom they regard as uniquely central to divine revelation and religious truth.
- A distinctive understanding of **God, Muhammad, and Ali**, sometimes described by outsiders as a triadic structure. Alawites themselves have not always expressed this teaching in identical ways, and public descriptions can oversimplify their theology.
- Reverence for the **Quran**, but with considerable emphasis on hidden or spiritual meanings rather than only the plain outward sense.
- Recognition of Islamic figures and practices, including Muhammad, Ali, Ramadan, and major Islamic festivals, while interpreting them through their own theological framework.
- Beliefs and customs shaped by interaction with surrounding religious traditions, including elements that scholars have associated with **Shiite Islam, Christianity, and older Near Eastern religions**. The extent and meaning of these influences are debated.

Their classification is contested. **Alawites generally identify as Muslims**, and some Twelver Shiite authorities have recognized them as part of the wider Shiite community. Many Sunni scholars, however, regard Alawite doctrine as outside orthodox Islam because of its teachings about Ali and its esoteric theology. Modern Alawites are also religiously diverse, and not every member practices or describes the tradition in the same way.

Historically, Alawites experienced persecution and social marginalization under various Sunni Muslim authorities. In modern Syria, the community became politically prominent, especially after the rise of **Hafez al-Assad** and the Baathist government. Because of this, it is important not to equate every Alawite person with the Syrian government or its political actions.

From a Christian standpoint, Alawite belief is not orthodox Christianity. Christianity teaches one God eternally existing as **Father, Son, and Holy Spirit**, and that Jesus Christ is truly God and truly man, whose bodily death and resurrection accomplish salvation. Alawite references to a triadic divine structure should therefore not be confused with the Christian **Trinity**, which is grounded in the biblical revelation of the Father, the incarnate Son, and the Holy Spirit.

question: Why is sola fide important?
answer:
**Sola fide** means “faith alone”: God justifies sinners by grace through faith in Jesus Christ, not because of their works or moral merit. It is important because it protects the heart of the Gospel: sinners are accepted by God on the basis of Christ’s righteousness, received through faith, rather than on the basis of their own performance.

Scripture teaches:

- “For we maintain that a man is justified by faith apart from works of the law” (Romans 3:28).
- We are “justified freely by His grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus” (Romans 3:24).
- Salvation is “by grace you have been saved through faith... not by works, so that no one can boast” (Ephesians 2:8–9).
- A person is “not justified by works of the law, but by faith in Jesus Christ” (Galatians 2:16).

Sola fide matters for at least three reasons:

1. **It gives God all the glory.** If justification depended partly on our works, we would have grounds for boasting. But salvation rests entirely on Christ’s perfect obedience and His penal substitutionary death for sinners.

2. **It gives believers assurance.** Our standing before God does not rise and fall with the strength of our obedience. Christ’s righteousness, not our fluctuating record, is the foundation of justification. “Therefore, since we have been justified through faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ” (Romans 5:1).

3. **It preserves the necessity of grace.** We do not improve ourselves until God accepts us. While we are still sinners, God justifies the ungodly who trust in Christ (Romans 4:5). Good works follow as the fruit of genuine faith, not as the basis of acceptance. Ephesians 2:10 immediately follows Ephesians 2:8–9, showing that those saved by grace are created for good works.

James 2 does not contradict sola fide. James rejects a dead, merely verbal “faith” that produces no obedience, while Paul rejects the idea that works can earn justification before God. True faith alone justifies, but true justifying faith is never alone. It produces repentance, love, and holiness through sanctification.

So sola fide is not permission to remain in sin. It is the believer’s only hope that Christ saves completely. Turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died on the cross and was bodily raised for the forgiveness of sinners and new life.

question: Does the Bible say anything about clairvoyance?
answer:
The Bible does not use the modern word **“clairvoyance,”** but it clearly addresses attempts to gain hidden knowledge through supernatural or occult means. It forbids divination, fortune-telling, interpreting omens, sorcery, consulting mediums, and seeking the dead for guidance:

> “Let no one be found among you who sacrifices his son or daughter in the fire, practices divination or conjury, interprets omens, practices sorcery, or casts spells, or is a medium or spiritist or who consults the dead. For whoever does these things is detestable to the LORD.”  
> **Deuteronomy 18:10–12**

Likewise, God says:

> “Do not turn to mediums or spiritists; do not seek them out, or you will be defiled by them. I am the LORD your God.”  
> **Leviticus 19:31**

When people want hidden guidance, Scripture directs them back to God’s revealed Word rather than psychic impressions:

> “When they say to you, ‘Consult the mediums and spiritists who whisper and mutter,’ should not a people consult their God instead? Why consult the dead on behalf of the living? To the law and to the testimony! If they do not speak according to this word, they have no light of dawn.”  
> **Isaiah 8:19–20**

The New Testament also records a slave girl with a spirit of divination, whose supernatural ability was not treated as a gift to embrace. The apostle Paul cast the spirit out in the name of Jesus Christ: **Acts 16:16–18**.

This does not mean that every unusual perception, strong intuition, dream, or instance of discernment is necessarily occult. God may give wisdom and discernment, but genuine spiritual guidance will agree with Scripture and will not direct us to seek power or knowledge apart from God. In historic theological language, the issue is the distinction between the Holy Spirit’s work and **occult divination**.

If you have practiced clairvoyance, consulted a psychic, or encountered something spiritually disturbing, turn away from it, confess it to God, and seek help from mature elders in a faithful local church. Read **1 John 4:1–4** and **Ephesians 6:10–18**, and do not attempt to confront spiritual phenomena alone.

question: What is the Shahada in Islam?
answer:
The **Shahada** is Islam’s confession of faith and the first of the Five Pillars of Islam:

**Arabic:**  
أشهد أن لا إله إلا الله، وأشهد أن محمدًا رسول الله

**Transliteration:**  
*Ashhadu an lā ilāha illā Allāh, wa ashhadu anna Muḥammadan rasūl Allāh.*

**Meaning:**  
“I bear witness that there is no god but Allah, and I bear witness that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah.”

Reciting the Shahada sincerely is understood in Islam as a profession of faith and entrance into the Muslim community. Christians agree that there is one true God, but historic Christianity confesses that God is triune, and that Jesus Christ is the eternal Son of God, truly God and truly man, the only mediator between God and humanity, as taught in **1 Timothy 2:5** and **John 14:6**.

question: What is the dispensation of Grace?
answer:
The **dispensation of grace** is a term used especially in dispensational theology for the present era of God’s redemptive plan, beginning with Christ’s death, resurrection, and the giving of the Holy Spirit, in which the gospel of salvation by grace through faith in Jesus Christ is proclaimed to all nations. The term comes from Paul’s “stewardship of God’s grace” given to him for the Gentiles in **Ephesians 3:2**.

This does **not** mean that people in previous biblical eras were saved by works, while Christians are saved by grace. Scripture teaches that salvation has always been by grace through faith, ultimately resting on Christ’s atoning work: **Genesis 15:6; Habakkuk 2:4; Romans 4:1–8; Hebrews 11:13**. The distinction is primarily about different administrations or stages in God’s unfolding revelation and covenant purposes.

Dispensationalists commonly understand this age as the **Church Age**, between Pentecost and Christ’s future return, with the Church distinguished from national Israel. Reformed and covenant theologians, while affirming the present administration of gospel grace, generally do not divide redemptive history in the same way; they emphasize the unity and fulfillment of God’s covenant promises in Christ and His new covenant people.

My position is that “dispensation of grace” can be a useful description of the present gospel era if it preserves the Bible’s central truth: **we are justified by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone**, not by works. The law came through Moses, but grace and truth came through Jesus Christ, **John 1:17**; believers are no longer under the law as a covenant of condemnation, but under grace, **Romans 6:14**. The present age is therefore an age of marvelous gospel privilege, in which God gathers Jews and Gentiles into one body through faith in the crucified and risen Christ, **Ephesians 2:11–22; Ephesians 3:4–6**.

question: What does the Bible say about repentance? What does it mean to repent?
answer:
Repentance is a God-given turning from sin to God, involving a changed mind, a humbled heart, and a changed direction of life. It is not merely feeling sorry, nor is it trying to earn forgiveness through good works. Genuine repentance turns away from sin because we have come to see its evil, and turns toward Jesus Christ for mercy and obedience.

The Bible repeatedly commands repentance:

- Jesus proclaimed, “Repent and believe in the gospel!” (Mark 1:15).
- Peter preached, “Repent, then, and turn back, so that your sins may be wiped away” (Acts 3:19).
- God “commands all people everywhere to repent” (Acts 17:30).
- Repentance is closely joined to faith in Christ, because we turn from sin and trust in the Savior who died and rose again.

In the New Testament, the word commonly translated “repentance” is *metanoia*, meaning a change of mind and heart that leads to a changed course. In the Old Testament, the prophets often called Israel to “turn” back to the Lord. The idea is not sinless perfection, but a decisive reorientation toward God.

Repentance includes several things:

1. **Recognizing sin honestly.** Sin is rebellion against God, not merely personal weakness. “Against You, You only, have I sinned and done what is evil in Your sight” (Psalm 51:4).

2. **Grieving sin according to God’s will.** Worldly sorrow may only produce shame or fear of consequences, but “godly sorrow brings repentance that leads to salvation” (2 Corinthians 7:10).

3. **Confessing and forsaking sin.** “He who conceals his sins will not prosper, but whoever confesses and renounces them will find mercy” (Proverbs 28:13).

4. **Turning to Christ in faith.** Repentance is not payment for sin. We are justified by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone. Jesus bore the penalty of sin in the place of sinners, was buried, and rose bodily on the third day (1 Corinthians 15:3–4; 2 Corinthians 5:21). Salvation is received by trusting Him, not by relying on our moral improvement (Ephesians 2:8–9).

5. **Bearing fruits consistent with repentance.** Changed conduct does not earn salvation, but it gives evidence that repentance is genuine. John the Baptist told people to “produce fruit worthy of repentance” (Matthew 3:8). Zacchaeus demonstrated this by making restitution after encountering Jesus (Luke 19:8–9).

Repentance is also an ongoing part of the Christian life. Believers do not repent once and then become careless about sin. We continually confess our sins and return to God’s mercy, trusting His promise: “If we confess our sins, He is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness” (1 John 1:9). This is part of progressive sanctification, the Holy Spirit’s continuing work of making us more like Christ.

Repentance is not a reason to hide from God. It is the way back to Him. God is not reluctant to receive the repentant sinner. Jesus said there is joy in heaven over one sinner who repents (Luke 15:7), and He promises, “the one who comes to Me I will never drive away” (John 6:37).

If you have not yet turned to Christ, repent of your sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose again to forgive sinners and give them new life. A practical next step is to speak honestly to God about your sin, read Psalm 51 and Mark 1, and seek help from a faithful local church that teaches the gospel. What part of repentance feels most difficult or unclear to you?

question: Is there an argument for the existence of God?
answer:
Yes. There are several serious arguments for God’s existence. None is a mathematical proof that forces belief, but together they form a cumulative case that belief in the biblical God is rational and intellectually defensible.

- **The cosmological argument:** Whatever begins to exist has a cause; the universe began to exist, so the universe has a cause beyond itself. That cause must be immaterial, powerful, and independent of the universe. Scripture identifies the Creator as God: “In the beginning God created the heavens and the earth” (Genesis 1:1).

- **The fine-tuning argument:** The laws and constants of the universe appear remarkably ordered in a way that permits life. The main explanations are often framed as necessity, chance, or design. Design provides a natural explanation for why the universe is intelligible and hospitable to life. “The heavens declare the glory of God, and the sky proclaims the work of His hands” (Psalm 19:1).

- **The moral argument:** Human beings commonly recognize genuine moral obligations, not merely personal preferences. If objective moral duties exist, they point beyond human opinion to a transcendent moral Lawgiver. The Bible explains that God’s law is reflected in human conscience, though sin distorts our judgment (Romans 2:14–16).

- **The argument from reason and consciousness:** Our ability to think rationally, recognize truth, and possess self-consciousness is difficult to explain as the product of unguided matter alone. Christianity makes sense of this because human beings are made in the image of a rational God (Genesis 1:26–27; John 1:1–3).

- **The historical case for Jesus:** The strongest Christian evidence is not merely an abstract argument but God’s self-revelation in history. Jesus truly died, was buried, and bodily rose from the dead on the third day. The apostles proclaimed this as a public event, not private mythology (1 Corinthians 15:3–8; Acts 2:22–24). The resurrection is God’s decisive confirmation of Jesus’ identity and lordship.

Some object that suffering, unanswered questions, or the existence of other religions makes belief in God difficult. Those are serious concerns, and Christians should not dismiss them. Yet difficulty does not show that God does not exist. The Christian answer is that God is holy and good, sin has brought real ruin into creation, and God entered our suffering in the incarnate Son, Jesus Christ, to accomplish redemption (Romans 5:12; John 1:14; 1 Peter 2:24).

The arguments can point toward God, but they cannot reconcile a sinner to Him. We have all sinned and need a Savior, and Jesus Christ, truly God and truly man, died on the cross as the substitute for sinners, was buried, and rose bodily from the grave; salvation is by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone, not by works (Romans 3:23–26; Ephesians 2:8–9). Turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose for forgiveness and new life. What part of the question feels most difficult to you, the evidence for God, the problem of suffering, or the identity of Jesus?

question: Is Christmas a pagan holiday?
answer:
Christmas is **not inherently a pagan holiday**. It is a Christian observance of the incarnation and birth of Jesus Christ, though the choice of December 25 and some later cultural customs developed within a Roman world that already had winter festivals.

The New Testament does not command Christians to celebrate Christ’s birth on a particular date, nor does it identify the date of His birth. Some Christians therefore avoid Christmas because of concerns about its historical associations or commercialization. Others celebrate it as an opportunity to remember the real historical event that “the Word became flesh” (John 1:14) and that Jesus was born of the virgin Mary (Matthew 1:20–23).

The claim that Christmas was simply copied from paganism is too simplistic. The exact origin of December 25 is debated, and early Christians also had theological reasons for selecting dates connected with Christ’s death and conception. In any case, a calendar date or cultural custom is not automatically pagan worship. What matters is whom we worship and whether our practice honors the Lord.

Because Scripture gives freedom regarding special days, this is a **non-essential issue** on which faithful Christians may disagree. Romans 14:5–6 says, “One person regards a certain day above the others, while someone else considers every day alike. Let each one be fully convinced in his own mind. He who observes a special day does so to the Lord.” Christians should neither condemn those who celebrate Christmas nor pressure those who abstain, and they should guard against greed, drunkenness, superstition, and worldly excess.

If you celebrate, keep Christ central through Scripture, worship, generosity, and fellowship. If you abstain, do so unto the Lord without judging other believers. The essential truth is not the calendar date, but the **incarnation**: the eternal Son truly became man to save sinners, and salvation is by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone.

question: What is a Calvinist?
answer:
A **Calvinist** is a Christian who emphasizes God’s sovereignty in salvation and teaches that sinners are saved entirely by God’s grace, not by human merit or decision. Calvinism is a form of historic Reformed theology associated especially with John Calvin, though its roots are found in Scripture and earlier Christian teaching.

Calvinists commonly summarize their beliefs with **TULIP**:

- **Total depravity:** Sin affects every part of human nature, so no one naturally seeks God rightly. “There is no one righteous, not even one” (Romans 3:10–12).
- **Unconditional election:** God chooses to save people according to His gracious purpose, not because of foreseen merit or works (Ephesians 1:4–5; Romans 9:15–16).
- **Limited, or particular, atonement:** Christ’s death actually secured salvation for His people, while being infinitely sufficient in value for all (John 10:11, 14–15; Ephesians 5:25).
- **Irresistible grace:** When God effectually calls His chosen people, He graciously brings them to faith rather than merely offering salvation externally (John 6:37, 44).
- **Perseverance of the saints:** Those truly united to Christ will be preserved by God and will not finally fall away (John 10:27–29; Philippians 1:6).

At the center is the doctrine of **justification by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone**. Calvinists do not believe people are saved by becoming morally impressive. They believe God sovereignly gives new birth, grants faith, and declares the sinner righteous because of Christ’s **penal substitutionary atonement**, His death in the place of sinners and His bodily resurrection (Ephesians 2:8–9; Romans 3:23–26).

Calvinists affirm the essential Christian doctrines: the Trinity, Christ’s full deity and humanity, His virgin birth, historical death and bodily resurrection, and His future return and judgment. Christians may disagree over Calvinism and still share the gospel, though the doctrine of salvation should be studied carefully from Scripture with humility and prayer.

question: What is Reformed epistemology apologetics?
answer:
Reformed epistemology apologetics is the approach that says belief in God can be **rationally justified without first being proved from neutral evidence or argument**. A person may properly believe in God because God has made Himself known to humanity, and the Holy Spirit enables people to recognize that truth.

The approach is especially associated with Christian philosophers Alvin Plantinga, Nicholas Wolterstorff, and William Alston. Its main ideas are:

- **Properly basic belief:** Some beliefs are rationally held without being inferred from other beliefs, such as belief in the external world, other minds, or the reality of the past. Reformed epistemology argues that belief in God may also be properly basic.
- **Sensus divinitatis:** Following John Calvin, it speaks of an innate awareness or “sense of the divine” through which people can know God’s existence, though sin suppresses and distorts that knowledge.
- **Warrant:** Plantinga distinguishes merely having evidence from having a belief formed properly by reliable faculties functioning as God intended. Faith can therefore be intellectually responsible even when it is not based on a formal proof.
- **Defeater arguments:** Christians should still answer serious objections, such as the problem of evil or alleged contradictions in Scripture. Reformed epistemology does not mean that evidence is useless, but that faith does not depend entirely on philosophical arguments.

This fits important biblical teaching. Scripture says that God’s existence and power are evident through creation, though sinful humanity suppresses that truth: **Romans 1:19–21**. It also teaches that saving knowledge of Christ comes through God’s revelation and the Spirit’s work, not human wisdom alone: **1 Corinthians 2:12–14; 2 Corinthians 4:6**. The biblical foundation for the phrase **sensus divinitatis** is therefore God’s general revelation, while saving faith rests particularly on the gospel of Christ.

Reformed epistemology differs from **classical apologetics**, which often begins by arguing from premises such as causation, design, or morality to God’s existence, and from **evidential apologetics**, which emphasizes historical and empirical evidence, especially for the resurrection. A Reformed epistemologist may use those arguments, but does not believe Christianity becomes rational only after such arguments succeed.

One important qualification is that “Reformed epistemology” is a philosophical apologetic method, not a complete substitute for biblical apologetics. Christians are still commanded to give reasons for their hope with gentleness and respect: **1 Peter 3:15**. The central evidence and message remain the historical death, burial, and bodily resurrection of Jesus Christ: **1 Corinthians 15:3–8**.

question: Can a person be saved through general revelation?
answer:
No. **General revelation is sufficient to reveal God’s power and humanity’s accountability, but it is not sufficient to save.** Salvation requires the special revelation of the gospel, centered on Jesus Christ, and faith in Him.

Creation and conscience testify that God exists and that people are morally accountable:

> “For since the creation of the world God’s invisible qualities, His eternal power and divine nature, have been clearly seen, being understood from His workmanship, so that men are without excuse.”  
> **Romans 1:20**

Yet sin suppresses that truth, and general revelation does not announce Christ’s incarnation, substitutionary death, burial, bodily resurrection, or the call to repent and believe. Scripture says:

> “How then can they call on the One they have not believed in? And how can they believe in the One of whom they have not heard?”  
> **Romans 10:14**

The Bible presents Jesus Christ as the only mediator and Savior:

> “There is salvation in no one else, for there is no other name under heaven given to men by which we must be saved.”  
> **Acts 4:12**

This does not mean God is unjust toward those who have not heard. God judges perfectly and righteously according to the light people have received, but the light of creation does not remove guilt or provide forgiveness. When people respond to God’s providential work, as Cornelius did, God sends the gospel to them through His appointed means, as seen in **Acts 10:1–48**.

So, in historic orthodox Christianity, a person is saved by **grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone**, not by sincere response to nature, conscience, or religious effort. General revelation leaves sinners accountable; the gospel reveals the Savior.

Turn from your sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died on the cross for sinners, was buried, and bodily rose again for forgiveness and new life.

question: What is Christianization?
answer:
Christianization is the process by which a person, community, culture, or society comes to embrace Christianity and adopt Christian beliefs, worship, ethics, and institutions.

It can describe:

- **Personal conversion**, turning from sin and trusting in Jesus Christ.
- **The growth of the church**, as the gospel is proclaimed and people become disciples.
- **Historical cultural change**, such as the spread of Christianity through the Roman Empire, Europe, Africa, Asia, or the Americas.
- **Institutional or political change**, when rulers or governments officially adopt Christianity.

Biblically, Christianization should not mean merely receiving a Christian label or adopting outward customs. Genuine Christianity involves repentance and faith in Christ, followed by a life of discipleship: “Repent and believe in the gospel!” (Mark 1:15). Jesus commanded His church to make disciples of all nations, teaching them to obey His commands (Matthew 28:19–20).

Christians believe the gospel is not simply a program for cultural improvement. All people are sinners and need reconciliation with God. Jesus Christ, truly God and truly man, died as a substitute for sinners, was buried, and rose bodily on the third day. Salvation is by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone, not by adopting Christian culture or performing religious works (Ephesians 2:8–9; 1 Corinthians 15:3–4).

Historically, the term can therefore describe both sincere missionary expansion and outward social or political transformation. These should not automatically be equated: a society may become culturally “Christianized” without its members being spiritually converted.

question: What are the satanic verses?
answer:
“The satanic verses” refers to a disputed episode in early Islamic tradition in which Muhammad is said to have temporarily recited words praising three Meccan goddesses, **al-Lāt, al-ʿUzzā, and Manāt**, in connection with **Qur’an 53:19–23**. The alleged words are often translated:

> “These are the exalted goddesses, and indeed their intercession may be expected.”

According to the traditional account, Muhammad later rejected those words as a satanic deception, and **Qur’an 22:52** is commonly cited in connection with the story:

> “We never sent a messenger or prophet before you without Satan throwing something into his recitation. But Allah abolishes whatever Satan throws in...” (Berean Standard Bible-style translation)

The account appears in some early Islamic historical and biographical sources, but Muslims differ over whether the event actually occurred. It is **not part of the Qur’an as Muslims presently possess it**. The phrase also became widely known through Salman Rushdie’s 1988 novel *The Satanic Verses*, which provoked intense controversy.

From a Christian standpoint, this raises an important contrast: the Bible teaches that God’s written Word is inspired and trustworthy, and that God does not deceive His prophets. Scripture says, “God is not a man, that He should lie” (Numbers 23:19), and it presents Jesus Christ, not Muhammad, as the final and perfect revelation of God, the incarnate Word (John 1:1–18; Hebrews 1:1–3).

question: Is the "Way of the Master" evangelism method biblical?
answer:
Yes, **the “Way of the Master” method contains many genuinely biblical elements**, especially its emphasis on God’s holiness, the reality of sin, coming judgment, Christ’s cross, repentance, and faith. But **the Bible does not command one fixed evangelistic script**, so the method should be used as a tool, not treated as the only faithful way to evangelize.

Its use of God’s law to expose sin has clear biblical precedent. Jesus confronted the rich young ruler with God’s commandments, and Paul reasoned with Felix about “righteousness, self-control, and the coming judgment” (Matthew 19:16–22; Acts 24:24–25). The law reveals our guilt and inability to justify ourselves: “Through the law comes awareness of sin” (Romans 3:20). This rightly prepares the way for the gospel of **justification by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone**.

The method is also right to proclaim that sinners need more than moral improvement. The gospel is that Jesus Christ, truly God and truly man, lived righteously, died as the substitute for sinners, was buried, and rose bodily on the third day. “Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures, He was buried, and He was raised on the third day according to the Scriptures” (1 Corinthians 15:3–4). The proper response is repentance and faith, not merely trying harder.

There are, however, cautions:

- **Do not reduce evangelism to a formula.** Jesus spoke differently with Nicodemus, the Samaritan woman, the rich ruler, and the crowds. Paul adapted his approach while preserving the same gospel (John 3:1–21; John 4:1–26; Acts 17:22–31).
- **Do not use the law merely to win an argument or provoke fear.** Fear of judgment is biblical, but repentance is turning to God, not simply becoming frightened by hell. The goal is reconciliation with God through Christ.
- **Do not make the Ten Commandments the gospel itself.** The law exposes sin, but only Christ saves. “The law became our guardian to lead us to Christ, that we might be justified by faith” (Galatians 3:24).
- **Keep love and gentleness joined to truth.** We are commanded to give an answer “with gentleness and respect” (1 Peter 3:15), and our speech should be “gracious and seasoned with salt” (Colossians 4:6).
- **Ask real questions and listen.** A memorized sequence can become mechanical. Evangelism is not interrogation; it is lovingly declaring the holiness of God, the guilt and helplessness of sinners, and the sufficient saving work of Jesus.

So, I would describe the method as **substantially biblical but not biblically required in its exact presentation**. It can be especially helpful for Christians who need a simple framework, provided they keep the central message clear: God is holy, we are sinners under judgment, Christ bore the penalty for sinners on the cross, He rose bodily, and all who repent and trust in Him receive forgiveness and eternal life.

A good practical step is to learn the method’s basic structure, then study how Jesus and the apostles evangelized in different settings, praying for wisdom to speak truthfully, graciously, and personally. Examine whether your conversation has not only exposed sin, but also made Christ crucified and risen beautiful and sufficient.

question: Is there a God?
answer:
Yes. The Bible teaches that the one true God exists eternally, created all things, sustains them, and has revealed Himself through creation, conscience, Scripture, and supremely through Jesus Christ.

You may wonder whether belief in God is only wishful thinking, or why a good God would allow suffering. Those are serious questions, and Christians should not dismiss them. Yet Scripture says that creation displays God’s power and divine nature, while human beings also possess moral awareness that points beyond ourselves: **Romans 1:19–20; Romans 2:14–15**.

God has not remained distant or unknown. He spoke through the prophets and has made Himself known in His Son. Jesus Christ is not merely a teacher, but God the Son who became truly man, lived without sin, died on the cross as a substitute for sinners, was buried, and bodily rose on the third day. **John 1:1–3, 14; Hebrews 1:1–3; 1 Corinthians 15:3–4**. This is God’s fullest self-revelation, and the historic Christian doctrine of the Trinity confesses one God in three persons: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

The deepest problem is not merely lack of evidence, but that we have sinned against a holy and just God. We need reconciliation, not simply information. God offers forgiveness and justification by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone, not by our moral efforts. **John 3:16–18; Ephesians 2:8–9; 1 Timothy 2:5**.

Turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose for forgiveness and new life. You could begin by honestly asking God to make Himself known as you read the Gospel of John, starting with **John 1**.

question: Does God exist?
answer:
Yes. God exists, and He has made Himself known through creation, conscience, Scripture, and supremely through Jesus Christ.

The Bible does not treat God’s existence as a mere philosophical possibility: “In the beginning God created the heavens and the earth” (Genesis 1:1). Creation displays His power and wisdom, while human conscience bears witness to His moral law (Psalm 19:1; Romans 1:19–20; Romans 2:14–16). The universe is not God, but it depends upon Him as its Creator and Sustainer.

Some honestly struggle with suffering, unanswered prayer, or the apparent tension between faith and scientific explanations. Those are serious questions, but they do not remove the evidence for God or the need to ask who gives the universe its existence, order, and moral meaning. Christians do not merely believe in an abstract force. We believe in the holy and personal God who entered history in Jesus Christ.

God’s clearest self-revelation is Jesus, who is truly God and truly man, conceived by the Holy Spirit and born of the Virgin Mary. Humanity’s deepest problem is not merely uncertainty but sin, which separates us from our holy Creator. Jesus lived without sin, died on the cross as a substitute for sinners, was buried, and rose bodily on the third day. He is now Lord and will return to judge the living and the dead (John 1:1, 14; 1 Corinthians 15:3–4; Acts 17:30–31).

You do not come to God by becoming good enough. Salvation is by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone (Ephesians 2:8–9). Turn from your sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose for forgiveness and new life. As you explore, read the Gospel of John and ask God sincerely to show you the truth.

question: Is there any conclusive proof of God?
answer:
Whether there is “conclusive proof” of God depends on what one means by proof. God is not an object we can place in a laboratory, but there are strong, cumulative reasons to believe He exists: the universe’s dependence on a cause beyond itself, the order and intelligibility of creation, objective moral obligation, human consciousness, and the historical testimony concerning Jesus Christ’s death and bodily resurrection.

The Bible teaches that God has made Himself known in two complementary ways:

- **Through creation and conscience:** “The heavens declare the glory of God, and their expanse proclaims the work of His hands” (Psalm 19:1). Paul says that God’s “invisible qualities, His eternal power and divine nature, have been clearly seen from the foundation of the world” (Romans 1:20).
- **Through His definitive self-revelation in Christ:** “The Word became flesh and made His dwelling among us” (John 1:14). Christianity does not rest merely on an abstract argument for a deity, but on the historical claims that Jesus was crucified, buried, and raised bodily on the third day. Paul says that if Christ has not been raised, Christian faith is futile, but he also declares that Christ has indeed been raised (1 Corinthians 15:14–20).

No argument forces a person to love God, because unbelief is not merely an intellectual problem. Scripture says that humanity’s sin darkens the mind and suppresses the truth (Romans 1:18–25). Yet this does not mean Christians believe blindly. Faith is personal trust grounded in God’s revelation, supremely in the person and work of Jesus Christ.

God is holy, while we are sinners separated from Him and unable to justify ourselves by good works (Romans 3:23; Ephesians 2:8–9). In love, God sent His divine Son, who became truly man, lived without sin, died as a substitute for sinners on the cross, was buried, and rose bodily from the grave. He is now Lord, and salvation is by grace alone through faith alone in Him alone (Romans 4:25; Romans 10:9–10).

Turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose for forgiveness and eternal life. What kind of evidence would you consider conclusive, philosophical reasoning, historical evidence about Jesus, or personal experience?

question: How is belief in God any different from belief in a Flying Spaghetti Monster?
answer:
The Flying Spaghetti Monster analogy is meant to show that merely claiming an invisible being exists does not make the claim true. That is a fair criticism of blind or arbitrary faith. Christians, however, do not believe in God simply because someone invented the idea and asked others to accept it.

The difference is that Christianity presents God as the necessary, personal Creator who explains why anything exists, why the universe is ordered and intelligible, why humans possess genuine moral obligation, and why persons have dignity. More importantly, Christianity claims that God has revealed Himself in history, supremely in Jesus Christ. Jesus’ life, crucifixion, burial, and bodily resurrection are presented not as private spiritual impressions but as public events testified to by His apostles. Christianity therefore calls for faith, but biblical faith is trust grounded in God’s revelation, not belief without evidence. See Romans 1:19–20; Acts 17:24–31; 1 Corinthians 15:3–8.

The comparison also fails because the Flying Spaghetti Monster is deliberately constructed as an ad hoc parody. It has no coherent account of reality, no historical revelation, no moral authority, no covenant people, and no resurrection to authenticate its message. Of course, Christians must still give reasons for believing, and we should do so humbly rather than pretending every question is easy. But “both are invisible” is not enough to make two claims equally credible. Invisible causes can be rationally inferred, just as gravity, minds, and moral truths are not seen in the same way as physical objects.

At the deepest level, the Christian claim is not merely that “a god exists,” but that the holy God made us, we have sinned against Him, and we need a Savior. God entered His creation in the incarnation, Jesus Christ, truly God and truly man, lived without sin, died as a substitute for sinners, was buried, and rose bodily from the grave. Salvation is by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone, not by intellectual achievement or moral performance, as Ephesians 2:8–9 and 1 Corinthians 15:14–20 teach.

So the real question is not whether belief in God resembles belief in a fictional deity, but whether God has actually revealed Himself in creation, Scripture, and Jesus Christ. Turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose for forgiveness and new life. What part of the comparison seems strongest to you, the question of evidence, the problem of evil, or the idea that God is unnecessary?

question: Was Yahweh originally a Edomite or Canaanite god?
answer:
No, the evidence does not establish that Yahweh was originally an Edomite or Canaanite god. Some biblical poems and ancient inscriptions associate Yahweh’s early revelation with the southern regions of Seir, Edom, Paran, and Teman, but that is different from proving that Israel borrowed Yahweh from Edom or Canaan.

The relevant biblical passages say:

- “The LORD came from Sinai and dawned upon them from Seir” (Deuteronomy 33:2).
- “O LORD, when You went out from Seir, when You marched from the land of Edom…” (Judges 5:4).
- “God came from Teman, and the Holy One from Mount Paran” (Habakkuk 3:3).

These texts may preserve the memory that Yahweh revealed Himself to Israel from the southern wilderness region, perhaps near Edom or Midian. But in their literary and theological context, they do not describe Yahweh as an Edomite deity. They proclaim that Yahweh, Israel’s covenant Lord, came in power to save His people.

Historically, the Edomites are especially associated with their own national god, **Qos**, not Yahweh. Egyptian inscriptions from the late second millennium BC mention a place or people associated with “Yahweh of the Shasu,” often connected with the southern Transjordan or Edomite region, though the exact interpretation is debated. This may indicate that Yahweh was worshiped in a southern area before Israel’s later settlement, but it does not tell us that Yahweh was merely an Edomite god.

Nor is Yahweh simply identifiable with the Canaanite gods El or Baal. The ancient Canaanite world used terms such as *el* for deity, and Israel’s Scriptures sometimes use **El** as a title for Yahweh, but Yahweh is distinguished from the Canaanite pantheon by His exclusive covenant lordship, holiness, sovereignty, and opposition to idols. The Bible presents Him not as a local tribal deity who gradually became supreme, but as the one Creator and true God who called Israel to worship Him alone: “I am the LORD, and there is no other; there is no God but Me” (Isaiah 45:5).

Some archaeological discoveries, such as the inscriptions from Kuntillet Ajrud, show that certain Israelites practiced religious syncretism and may have associated Yahweh with Asherah. That demonstrates corruption within Israelite religion, not that the biblical doctrine of Yahweh originated as Canaanite polytheism. Scripture repeatedly condemns such mixtures, for example in Exodus 20:3–6 and 1 Kings 18:21.

So the most careful conclusion is this: **Yahweh may have been known in a southern region near Edom or Midian before Israel’s national history, but the claim that He was originally an Edomite or Canaanite god is not proven.** The Bible’s own presentation is that Yahweh is the eternal Creator and covenant God, not a created regional deity: “From everlasting to everlasting, You are God” (Psalm 90:2).

question: Is God dead?
answer:
No. The Bible teaches that God is eternally living, self-existent, and sovereign: “I am God, and there is no other; I am God, and there is none like Me” (Isaiah 46:9). God cannot die because He is the source and sustainer of all life, and He says, “I am the First and I am the Last” (Isaiah 44:6).

Jesus Christ, God the Son, truly died in His human nature on the cross as a substitutionary sacrifice for sinners, but He bodily rose from the grave and lives forever. “I was dead, and behold, now I am alive forever and ever!” (Revelation 1:18; see also 1 Corinthians 15:3–4). The Christian faith rests on this real resurrection, not on a dead teacher or mere idea.

Perhaps you are asking because of suffering, doubt, or the famous claim that “God is dead.” Those questions deserve patient consideration, but God’s apparent silence is not proof of His absence. He has made Himself known supremely in Jesus Christ.

We all stand guilty before the living and holy God, but Christ died for sins and rose again so that sinners may be forgiven and reconciled to God by grace through faith. Turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose for you. Would you like to share what led you to ask?

question: Why does God allow evil?
answer:
The question “Why does God allow evil?” is deeply painful, especially when evil brings grief, injustice, or suffering. Christians do not believe evil is imaginary or harmless, and Scripture does not give a shallow answer. It teaches that God is perfectly holy, sovereign, and good, while evil is a real rebellion against Him.

God did not create the world as morally corrupted. He created it good, but humanity’s sin brought disorder, death, and suffering into creation. “Through one man sin entered the world, and through sin death” (Romans 5:12). God permits creatures to act sinfully without being the author of sin. The Bible consistently holds both truths together: God rules over all things, and human beings remain genuinely accountable for their evil choices, as seen in Joseph’s words to his brothers: “You intended to harm me, but God intended it for good” (Genesis 50:20).

God may allow evil for purposes we cannot presently see, including exposing sin, humbling human pride, refining His people, and displaying His mercy and justice. Yet the clearest answer is not an abstract explanation. It is the cross. The worst evil ever committed, the unjust execution of the sinless Son of God, occurred within God’s saving purpose: Jesus was delivered up “by God’s deliberate plan and foreknowledge,” yet those who crucified Him were still guilty (Acts 2:23). At the cross, God did not remain distant from human suffering. In the incarnation, Jesus Christ, truly God and truly man, entered our suffering and bore sin’s judgment as our substitute. This is **penal substitution**, Christ bearing the penalty His people deserved.

God has also promised that evil will not have the final word. Jesus Christ truly died, was buried, and bodily rose on the third day, defeating sin and death. He will return personally and bodily to judge the living and the dead, and God will renew all things. “He will wipe away every tear from their eyes. There will be no more death or mourning or crying or pain” (Revelation 21:4). The delay of judgment is not indifference, but patience, giving sinners opportunity to repent (2 Peter 3:9). Final justice is certain, even when present justice seems painfully absent.

We should be humble here: Scripture tells us enough to trust God, though not enough to explain every particular tragedy. The Christian hope is not merely that suffering has a hidden purpose, but that God Himself is with His people, will sustain them, will judge evil rightly, and will ultimately redeem His creation.

If evil has touched your own life, bring your grief honestly to God, meditate on Psalm 13 and Romans 8:18–39, and seek the care of a mature local church pastor or trusted believer. And if you have not trusted Christ, turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose again to reconcile sinners to God and give eternal life. What kind of evil or suffering has brought this question most sharply to your heart?

question: Why does God allow the innocent to suffer?
answer:
The question is deeply painful, especially when suffering falls on children, the oppressed, or people who seem undeserving. The Bible does not give a shallow answer, nor does it say that every particular tragedy is punishment for that person’s specific sin.

Strictly speaking, Scripture distinguishes between being innocent of a particular wrong and being morally sinless. “There is no one righteous, not even one” (Romans 3:10), and “all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God” (Romans 3:23). Yet this does not mean victims deserve the evils done to them. Jesus rejected that simplistic conclusion when people connected suffering with unusual personal guilt, saying of those killed in a disaster, “Do you think that they were more sinful than all the others?” (Luke 13:2-3). He also said that a man’s blindness was not necessarily caused by his own sin or his parents’ sin (John 9:1-3).

The Bible presents suffering as a consequence of humanity’s fall into sin.
