Through Adam’s rebellion, sin and death entered the world, bringing corruption not only into human hearts but into creation itself (Genesis 3:16-19; Romans 5:12; Romans 8:20-22). God is not the author of evil, and He does not delight in cruelty. Nevertheless, in His sovereignty, He permits evil for a time while working out purposes that are often hidden from us. Job shows that we may not know the reason for a particular suffering, but we can know that God remains righteous and worthy of trust (Job 1:21-22; Job 38:1-4; Job 42:5-6).

The clearest answer is found not in an explanation but in the cross. Jesus Christ, the truly innocent and sinless One, suffered unjustly, was crucified, buried, and bodily raised from the dead. His suffering was not meaningless: by penal substitution, He bore the judgment deserved by sinners so that those who trust Him may be reconciled to God (Isaiah 53:4-6; 1 Peter 3:18; 1 Corinthians 15:3-4). God did not remain distant from human grief. In Christ, He entered it, bore it, and overcame it.

Christian hope also rests on God’s final judgment and the renewal of all things. Every injustice will be answered, and God will ultimately remove death, mourning, crying, and pain (Revelation 21:3-5). Until then, Christians are called to weep with those who weep, defend the vulnerable, pray, and do tangible good rather than offer careless explanations (Romans 12:15; James 1:27).

If you are suffering personally, bring your honest grief to God, read Psalm 13 and Romans 8:18-39, and seek support from a faithful local church and trusted believers. You do not have to pretend that the pain is small in order to trust that God is good.

Our deepest problem is not merely suffering but sin and separation from our holy Creator, and our deepest hope is Jesus Christ, who died for sinners and rose bodily to give forgiveness and new life. Turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who suffered and rose for you.

question: Why won't God heal amputees?
answer:
That is a painful and serious question. The honest Christian answer is that we do not know why God has not ordinarily restored amputated limbs, and we should not pretend that easy explanations remove the sorrow.

The Bible does not teach that God is unable to heal amputees. He is sovereign and can perform any miracle He pleases. But it also does not promise that every faithful person will be physically healed in this present age. Jesus healed many people, yet not every sick person in Israel was healed. His miracles were signs of His kingdom and identity, not a guarantee that suffering would disappear before His return. Jesus Himself said, “It was not that this man sinned, or his parents,” when speaking of a man born blind, rejecting the idea that disability automatically reveals personal sin, John 9:1–3.

The deeper biblical explanation is that creation is presently subject to the curse of sin and death: “We know that the whole creation has been groaning together until now,” Romans 8:22. Christians are not promised escape from every bodily loss now, but we are promised resurrection and complete restoration when Christ returns. Jesus will “transform our lowly bodies to be like His glorious body,” Philippians 3:20–21. That hope is not merely improved circumstances, but bodily redemption through Christ.

This does not make an amputee’s grief small. God does not ask people to call evil good or to suppress lament. Scripture gives us permission to cry, “How long, O LORD?” Psalm 13:1–2, while still trusting His character. And God has entered our suffering personally in the incarnation: Jesus Christ is truly God and truly man, He suffered and died on the cross as the sin-bearing substitute for His people, was buried, and bodily rose from the dead. The resurrection is God’s pledge that suffering and death will not have the final word.

So I would not say, “God does not heal amputees.” I would say, “God has not promised to heal every injury in this age, though He remains able to heal, and He has promised the final resurrection of all who belong to Christ.” If this question is personal, bring the sorrow honestly to God, read Romans 8:18–25, and speak with a compassionate local pastor or mature believer who will listen rather than offer clichés.

question: Is Jesus real?
answer:
Yes. Jesus of Nazareth was a real first-century Jewish man who lived in Roman Judea, was crucified under Pontius Pilate, and was proclaimed by His earliest followers as risen from the dead. The New Testament presents Him not as a legend, but as the eternal Son of God who truly became man, the hypostatic union of full deity and full humanity (John 1:1–3, 14; Philippians 2:6–8).

The central Christian claim is that Jesus died for sinners, was buried, and bodily rose on the third day (1 Corinthians 15:3–4). Humanity’s deepest problem is not merely ignorance but sin and separation from a holy God, and Jesus came to save His people through His substitutionary death and resurrection (Romans 3:23–26; Romans 4:25).

Turn from your sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose again to give forgiveness and eternal life. What makes you ask whether Jesus is real, historical evidence, His identity, or whether you can know Him personally?

question: Did Jesus really exist? Is there any historical evidence of Jesus Christ?
answer:
Yes. Jesus of Nazareth really existed, and His existence is among the best-established facts of ancient history. The evidence does not depend only on the New Testament.

Several early sources refer to Him or to the movement founded by Him:

- **Tacitus**, a Roman historian writing around AD 115–117, said that “Christus” was executed under Pontius Pilate during the reign of Tiberius and that His followers spread from Judea to Rome.
- **Josephus**, a first-century Jewish historian, referred to “James, the brother of Jesus, who was called Christ” in *Antiquities* 20.9.1. He also included a longer reference to Jesus in *Antiquities* 18.3.3, though that passage appears to have been edited by later Christian copyists. Most historians still accept that it preserves an authentic reference to Jesus.
- **Pliny the Younger**, a Roman governor, wrote around AD 112 that Christians worshiped Christ “as a god.”
- **The New Testament documents** were written within the first century, beginning with Paul’s letters only a few decades after Jesus’ death. Paul personally knew Peter and James, “the Lord’s brother” (Galatians 1:18–19).

The historical evidence especially supports that Jesus was a Jewish teacher, gathered disciples, was crucified under Pontius Pilate, and that His followers immediately proclaimed that He had risen from the dead. The earliest Christian testimony says:

> “For what I received I passed on to you as of first importance: that Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures, that He was buried, that He was raised on the third day according to the Scriptures, and that He appeared to Cephas and then to the Twelve. After that He appeared to more than five hundred brothers at once.”  
> **1 Corinthians 15:3–6**

History can establish that these claims were made very early, by people who claimed to have witnessed the risen Jesus. The Bible also teaches that the resurrection was not merely a spiritual idea or metaphor, but a bodily event. Luke presents his Gospel as an orderly account based on eyewitness testimony (Luke 1:1–4), and Jesus says after His resurrection, “Touch Me and see, for a spirit does not have flesh and bones as you see I have” (Luke 24:39).

So the question is not seriously whether Jesus existed. The deeper question is whether He truly is who He claimed to be: the incarnate Son of God, crucified as a substitute for sinners and bodily raised from the dead. Because all people have sinned and need a Savior, turn from your sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose again to bring forgiveness and new life. What aspect would you like to examine more closely, the ancient sources, the reliability of the Gospels, or the evidence for the resurrection?

question: What is the Skeptics' Annotated Bible?
answer:
The **Skeptic’s Annotated Bible** is a website and printed reference work, created by **Steve Wells**, that presents biblical passages alongside skeptical comments. It highlights what the author considers contradictions, historical or scientific difficulties, morally troubling commands, failed prophecies, and inconsistencies within the Bible.

It is **not a neutral academic Bible commentary**. It approaches Scripture from an explicitly skeptical, non-Christian standpoint and often treats difficult passages as evidence against biblical inspiration and inerrancy. Its annotations can therefore be useful for identifying questions critics raise, but they do not by themselves establish that the Bible is mistaken.

Christians should examine each claim in its **literary, historical, and immediate biblical context**. Apparent contradictions may involve different witnesses emphasizing different details, translation issues, figures of speech, or passages being separated from their context. Scripture itself teaches that it is “God-breathed” and authoritative for teaching and correction, **2 Timothy 3:16–17**, while also commending careful examination, **Acts 17:11**. The Bible’s central message is not merely a collection of disputed details, but God’s saving work through Jesus Christ, whose death and bodily resurrection are the foundation of the Christian faith, **1 Corinthians 15:3–4**.

question: Is the Bible a fairy tale?
answer:
No. The Bible is not a fairy tale. It is a collection of writings in different genres, including history, poetry, prophecy, wisdom, letters, and parables. Some passages use figurative language, but the Bible presents its central events, especially Jesus’ incarnation, crucifixion, burial, and bodily resurrection, as real events in history.

Luke begins his Gospel by saying he investigated the events carefully so that readers could know their certainty, Luke 1:1–4. The apostle Peter likewise wrote, “We did not follow cleverly devised fables” when proclaiming Christ’s power and coming, 2 Peter 1:16. Paul identified the gospel as historical testimony: Christ “died for our sins according to the Scriptures,” was buried, was raised on the third day, and appeared to many witnesses, 1 Corinthians 15:3–8.

Some people call the Bible a fairy tale because miracles seem impossible or because they have encountered poor interpretations or hypocrisy from Christians. Those concerns should be considered honestly, but rejecting a claim merely because it is extraordinary does not establish that it is false. The Christian claim is that the holy God acted in history, culminating in the resurrection of Jesus Christ.

The Bible also tells us why this matters: humanity is sinful and separated from God, but Jesus, truly God and truly man, bore sin’s judgment on the cross and rose bodily to give forgiveness and life. Salvation is by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone, not by trying to become good enough, Ephesians 2:8–9; Romans 5:8; Romans 10:9.

Turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose for you, for forgiveness and new life. What part of the Bible seems most like a fairy tale to you, the miracles, the creation account, or something else?

question: Is the Bible mind control?
answer:
No, the Bible is not “mind control.” It calls people to hear truth, examine its claims, repent, and willingly trust God, rather than surrendering their reasoning to human manipulation.

The Bible even commends careful examination: “Now the Bereans were more noble-minded than the Thessalonians, for they received the message with great eagerness and examined the Scriptures every day to see if these teachings were true” (Acts 17:11). Jesus also invited honest examination of His works and teaching, saying, “If anyone is willing to do His will, he will know whether My teaching is from God” (John 7:17).

At the same time, Christianity does not treat the Bible as merely one opinion among many. It claims to be God’s authoritative Word, and God commands repentance and faith. The biblical idea is not the erasure of the mind, but its renewal: “Do not be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind” (Romans 12:2). This is part of sanctification, the Spirit’s work of making believers more like Christ.

Manipulative religion can certainly misuse the Bible by forbidding questions, isolating people, demanding unquestioning loyalty to a leader, or using fear and shame to control them. Those practices are not justified by Scripture. Jesus condemned domineering leadership, and He taught His disciples to serve rather than lord authority over others (Mark 10:42–45).

The Christian claim is that God does not compel belief through deception, but reveals truth and calls sinners to respond. Since all people are morally accountable before a holy God, the Bible confronts us with our sin and need for a Savior. Jesus Christ, truly God and truly man, died as a substitute for sinners, was buried, and bodily rose from the dead. Salvation is by grace alone through faith alone in Him, not by works. Turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone for forgiveness and new life.

What specifically has made the Bible seem like mind control to you, its teachings, the behavior of Christians, or the way someone presented it?

question: Does the Bible contain errors, contradictions, or discrepancies?
answer:
The Bible, in its original writings, contains no errors or contradictions because it is breathed out by God, who cannot lie. Christians call this **biblical inerrancy**: Scripture is wholly true in all that its human authors intended to affirm, while still using poetry, symbolism, rounded numbers, ordinary observational language, and different literary styles.

Scripture says, “All Scripture is God-breathed” (2 Timothy 3:16), that “every word of God is flawless” (Proverbs 30:5), and that Jesus prayed, “Your word is truth” (John 17:17). The Holy Spirit guided the prophets and apostles as they wrote (2 Peter 1:20–21), so the Bible’s ultimate author is God, even though He used distinct human authors and personalities.

Some passages do present **apparent discrepancies**, such as:

- Differences in the wording and arrangement of the four Gospel accounts.
- The reported numbers in 2 Samuel 24:9 and 1 Chronicles 21:5.
- The accounts of Judas’s death in Matthew 27:5 and Acts 1:18.
- Variations among ancient manuscript copies.

These should not be dismissed carelessly. They require attention to context, genre, Hebrew and Greek wording, ancient ways of recording events, and the distinction between what a passage explicitly says and what readers assume it must mean. A difference in detail is not automatically a contradiction. For example, several witnesses may truthfully report the same event while emphasizing different details.

There are also **textual variants** among surviving manuscript copies, usually involving spelling, word order, or small omissions and additions. This is why modern Bibles sometimes include footnotes. Such variants do not mean that the original Scriptures contained errors, nor do they overturn any central Christian doctrine. The original writings given through the prophets and apostles were without error, while copyists and translators, being human, could make mistakes.

At the same time, Christians should be humble: not every difficult passage has a universally agreed explanation, and some proposed harmonizations are stronger than others. But the proper conclusion is not that the Bible contradicts itself. It is that our understanding may be incomplete. Scripture remains the final authority, and apparent difficulties should be investigated rather than used as evidence against God’s truth.

A helpful posture is to read difficult passages in their immediate context, compare parallel accounts, examine reliable translations and textual notes, and ask a mature pastor or elder for help. “The sum of Your word is truth” (Psalm 119:160).

question: What is Christian apologetics?
answer:
Christian apologetics is the reasoned defense of the truth of Christianity and the Christian faith. It is not apologizing for believing in Jesus, but giving thoughtful answers to honest questions and objections about God, Scripture, Christ, the resurrection, and the Gospel.

The word comes from the Greek *apologia*, meaning a defense or reasoned answer. Scripture says, “But in your hearts sanctify Christ as Lord. Always be prepared to give a defense to everyone who asks you the reason for the hope that is in you. But respond with gentleness and respect” (1 Peter 3:15).

Christian apologetics may address questions such as:

- Does God exist?
- Can we trust the Bible?
- Did Jesus truly rise bodily from the dead?
- Why does God allow suffering?
- Is Jesus really God and the only Savior?
- Is Christianity intellectually credible?

Its purpose is not merely to win arguments. Apologetics serves the truth, removes obstacles to faith, strengthens believers, and points people to Jesus Christ. Reasoned evidence cannot regenerate a sinner, because salvation is God’s work, but the Holy Spirit uses truth proclaimed faithfully. The Gospel remains central: human beings are sinners separated from a holy God, Jesus Christ became truly man while remaining truly God, died as the substitute for sinners, was buried, rose bodily on the third day, and now reigns as Lord. We are justified by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone, not by intellectual achievement or moral works (1 Corinthians 15:3–4; Romans 3:23–26; Ephesians 2:8–9).

A practical starting point is to study the Gospel of John, especially John 20:30–31, and learn to explain clearly why you trust Christ while speaking with humility, patience, and love.

question: Does the Bible call Christians to defend the faith / argue for the faith?
answer:
Yes. The Bible calls Christians to **contend for and give a reasoned defense of the faith**, but it forbids quarrelsome, proud, or hostile arguing.

Jude 1:3 says believers should “contend earnestly for the faith entrusted once for all to the saints.” Likewise, Peter commands, “in your hearts sanctify Christ as Lord. Always be prepared to give a defense to everyone who asks you the reason for the hope that is in you. But respond with gentleness and respect” (1 Peter 3:15).

This defense of Christianity is often called **apologetics**, from the Greek word *apologia*, meaning a reasoned defense. Paul modeled this by “reasoning and persuading” people about the kingdom of God and Jesus Christ (Acts 17:2–4; Acts 17:16–34; Acts 26:24–29). He also described himself as appointed “for the defense and confirmation of the gospel” (Philippians 1:7).

At the same time, defending truth must not become sinful contention. Christians are told:

- “The Lord’s servant must not be quarrelsome, but must be kind to everyone, able to teach, and forbearing” (2 Timothy 2:24–25).
- “Avoid foolish controversies and genealogies and arguments and quarrels about the law, because these are unprofitable and useless” (Titus 3:9).
- “The anger of man does not bring about the righteousness that God desires” (James 1:20).

So, Christians should **argue for the faith**, meaning they should explain, support, and defend the truth of the gospel. They should not argue merely to win, humiliate, or display knowledge. The goal is faithfulness to Christ and, where God grants it, the rescue of those trapped in error: “Then you will know how to answer everyone” (Colossians 4:6).

A practical next step is to study a short passage such as 1 Peter 3:13–17, learn to explain the gospel clearly, and ask God for the courage, wisdom, gentleness, and love to speak when opportunities arise.

question: What are the cosmological arguments for the existence of God?
answer:
Cosmological arguments reason from the existence, beginning, contingency, or order of the universe to the existence of God. They do not all prove every Christian doctrine by themselves, but they provide philosophical support for the conclusion that the universe depends upon a transcendent, necessary, intelligent, and powerful Creator.

### 1. The Kalam cosmological argument

The Kalam argument reasons:

1. Whatever begins to exist has a cause.
2. The universe began to exist.
3. Therefore, the universe has a cause beyond the universe.

If the universe includes all matter, energy, space, and time, then its cause cannot be merely another physical object within the universe. The cause must be transcendent of the physical universe, immaterial, immensely powerful, and capable of bringing the universe into existence.

This accords with the biblical opening, “In the beginning God created the heavens and the earth” (Genesis 1:1), and with the New Testament teaching that “all things were created by Him” (John 1:3; Colossians 1:16).

### 2. The argument from contingency

A contingent thing is something that exists but could have failed to exist. The universe appears contingent because it does not contain within itself an explanation for why it exists rather than not existing.

The argument is:

1. Contingent things require an explanation for their existence.
2. The universe is contingent.
3. Therefore, the universe requires an explanation beyond itself.
4. That ultimate explanation must be a necessary being, one whose existence does not depend on anything else.

The Bible expresses this dependence in the words, “For from Him and through Him and to Him are all things” (Romans 11:36), and, “He Himself gives everyone life and breath and everything else” (Acts 17:25).

This argument points especially toward God as the necessary ground of all being, not merely as a powerful event-causer.

### 3. The argument from efficient causation

Everything that comes into existence or undergoes change depends upon something else as its cause. A chain of dependent causes cannot ultimately explain itself if every member depends on a prior member.

Therefore, there must be a first, uncaused cause that gives existence and causal power to everything else. Thomas Aquinas famously developed this form of the argument, though its basic idea is found in classical Christian theology.

The biblical term often used to summarize this truth is **creation**, meaning that God is not one being among others but the One upon whom all created beings depend. “In Him all things hold together” (Colossians 1:17).

### 4. The argument from motion or change

In older philosophical language, “motion” means change, not merely movement through space. Things that change are moved from potentiality to actuality by something already actual in the relevant respect. For example, wood that could become hot becomes hot through contact with something already hot.

A series of changes ultimately requires a source that is not itself dependent upon another changer. This leads to the concept of God as the **unmoved mover**, or more precisely, the One who possesses fullness of actuality and does not depend on anything outside Himself.

Scripture teaches that God is immutable and self-existent: “I, the LORD, do not change” (Malachi 3:6); “I AM WHO I AM” (Exodus 3:14).

### 5. The argument from temporal succession

Past events are formed by successive addition. If the universe had an actually infinite number of past events, it would be difficult to explain how the present moment could ever be reached through the completion of an infinite temporal sequence.

Thus, the argument concludes that the past is finite and that the universe had a beginning, requiring a cause beyond time and space.

This is closely related to the Kalam argument and fits the biblical teaching that God created time and the world, rather than merely existing as part of an eternal physical process (Genesis 1:1; Hebrews 11:3).

### What these arguments establish

Taken together, cosmological arguments point toward a God who is:

- Necessary rather than contingent
- Uncaused rather than dependent
- Eternal or beyond temporal limitation
- Immaterial, since matter and space are part of the created order
- Powerful enough to create the universe
- The sustaining ground of all existence

They do not, by themselves, fully establish the Trinity, the incarnation, or the gospel. Those truths are known through God’s special revelation in Scripture, culminating in Jesus Christ. The God inferred as the Creator is the God who has revealed Himself personally and savingly in Christ: “In the beginning was the Word... Through Him all things were made” (John 1:1–3).

Cosmological arguments therefore support the truth that the universe is not self-explanatory, but Christian faith rests ultimately not on abstract reasoning alone. It rests on God’s revelation, especially the historical death, burial, and bodily resurrection of Jesus Christ (1 Corinthians 15:3–4).

question: What is the purpose of the church?
answer:
The church is the gathered people of God, not merely a building or weekly meeting. Its chief purpose is to glorify God by worshiping Him, proclaiming the gospel of Jesus Christ, making disciples, and displaying God’s holy love to the world.

Scripture gives several connected purposes:

- **Worship God and proclaim His excellencies.** The church gathers to praise God, pray, hear His Word, and celebrate the Lord’s Supper. “Through Him, then, let us continually offer to God a sacrifice of praise” (Hebrews 13:15; see also Acts 2:42).
- **Preach the gospel.** Christ commissioned His church to make disciples of all nations, baptizing them and teaching them to obey His commands (Matthew 28:18–20). The gospel centers on Christ’s substitutionary death for sinners and His bodily resurrection.
- **Build up believers toward maturity.** Pastors and teachers equip Christians for ministry so that the body grows into spiritual maturity in Christ (Ephesians 4:11–16). This includes sanctification, the Spirit’s ongoing work of making believers more like Jesus.
- **Live in fellowship and mutual care.** Believers are to bear one another’s burdens, encourage one another, share generously, and practice genuine love (Acts 2:42–47; Galatians 6:2; Hebrews 10:24–25).
- **Guard holiness and truth.** The church teaches sound doctrine, practices loving discipline, and protects the purity of Christ’s people (1 Timothy 3:15; Matthew 18:15–17).
- **Serve neighbors and show mercy.** Christians are called to care for the needy and do good, especially toward fellow believers, as an expression of the gospel (Galatians 6:10; James 1:27).

In short, the church exists **to glorify God, proclaim Christ, make disciples, nurture believers, and bear faithful witness in the world**. A practical response is to join a faithful local church where you can regularly hear Scripture, worship, receive the ordinances, serve others, and grow alongside fellow Christians.

question: What is the Moral argument for the existence of God?
answer:
The **moral argument** reasons from the reality of objective moral truth to the existence of God:

1. **Objective moral values and duties exist.**  
   Some things are truly good or evil, right or wrong, regardless of what an individual or society believes. For example, torturing an innocent child for pleasure would be morally wrong even if a culture approved of it.

2. **Objective moral values and duties require an adequate foundation.**  
   Mere personal preference, social convention, or biological instinct can explain why people hold moral beliefs, but they do not make those beliefs objectively binding.

3. **God is the best foundation for objective morality.**  
   A holy, personal, and transcendent God provides the basis for moral obligation and human dignity.

4. **Therefore, God exists.**

In a compact form:

> If objective moral values and duties exist, God exists.  
> Objective moral values and duties do exist.  
> Therefore, God exists.

The argument does not mean that atheists cannot recognize moral truths or behave morally. It asks a deeper question: **What makes moral obligations objectively real and binding upon everyone?** Evolution may help explain how our moral instincts developed, but explaining the origin of a belief is not the same as explaining why the belief is objectively true.

The Bible gives this moral reality a clear foundation. Humanity is made in God’s image, which grounds human dignity, and God’s law is written on the conscience:

> “For when Gentiles, who do not have the law, do by nature what the law requires, they are a law to themselves, even though they do not have the law. They show that the work of the law is written on their hearts, their consciences also bearing witness, and their thoughts either accusing or defending them.”  
> Romans 2:14–15

God is not merely one moral agent among others. He is holy by nature, and His character is the standard of goodness. This avoids the classic dilemma, “Is something good because God commands it, or does God command it because it is good?” Biblically, goodness is neither arbitrary nor above God. It is rooted in who God eternally is. Jesus said, “No one is good except God alone” (Mark 10:18).

The moral argument also exposes our guilt. We do not merely fail to know moral truth, we knowingly violate it. Scripture says, “For all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God” (Romans 3:23). The moral law therefore points not only to God’s existence but also to our need for mercy.

Christians believe that mercy is found in Jesus Christ, who is truly God and truly man. He lived the righteous life we have failed to live, died on the cross as a substitute for sinners, was buried, and rose bodily on the third day. God’s justice and love meet in Christ’s **penal substitutionary atonement**, and sinners are justified by grace alone through faith alone in Him, not by their moral performance (Romans 3:21–26; 1 Corinthians 15:3–4; Ephesians 2:8–9).

Turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose again to reconcile sinners to God.

question: What is Ecclesiology?
answer:
Ecclesiology is the branch of Christian theology that studies the church, including its nature, purpose, leadership, ordinances, worship, mission, and relationship to Christ.

The word comes from the Greek *ekklesia*, meaning “assembly” or “church.” Scripture presents the church as both the worldwide people redeemed by Christ and the local congregation gathered for worship, teaching, fellowship, the Lord’s Supper, prayer, and mission. Christ is the church’s Head, and believers are members of His body, called to build one another up in love (Matthew 16:18; Acts 2:42; 1 Corinthians 12:27; Ephesians 1:22–23; Ephesians 4:11–16).

Ecclesiology therefore asks practical questions such as:

- Who belongs to the church?
- What authority does the church have?
- How should a local church be governed?
- What are the responsibilities of pastors, elders, and members?
- What are baptism and the Lord’s Supper?
- How should the church worship, disciple believers, evangelize, and practice discipline?

Historic Christians agree that Christ has one true church, though they differ on secondary matters such as church government, baptism, and the Lord’s Supper. From a Reformed Baptist perspective, a local church is a congregation of professing believers who covenant together under Christ, are led by qualified elders, practice believer’s baptism by immersion, observe the Lord’s Supper, and submit to the authority of Scripture (Matthew 28:19–20; Acts 2:41–42; 1 Timothy 3:1–13; 1 Peter 5:1–4).

question: What is the Teleological argument for the existence of God?
answer:
The **teleological argument** is an argument for God’s existence from **order, purpose, and apparent design in the universe**. “Teleological” comes from the Greek word *telos*, meaning “end,” “purpose,” or “goal.”

A common form is:

1. The universe displays order, intelligibility, and conditions remarkably suited for life.
2. Such purposeful order is best explained by an intelligent designer rather than by unguided forces alone.
3. Therefore, an intelligent Designer exists, whom Christians identify as God.

The argument is often illustrated by analogy: if you found a working watch, you would infer a watchmaker because its coordinated parts serve a purpose. In a similar way, the intricate order of nature and the universe points beyond itself to the wisdom of its Creator. Modern versions often focus on **fine-tuning**, the observation that many physical conditions appear precisely suited for life.

The Bible does not present creation as self-explanatory or purposeless. It teaches that God made and continually sustains all things:

> “The heavens declare the glory of God, and the sky proclaims the work of His hands.”  
> **Psalm 19:1**

> “For since the creation of the world God’s invisible qualities, His eternal power and divine nature, have been clearly seen, being understood from His workmanship, so that men are without excuse.”  
> **Romans 1:20**

Thus, the teleological argument corresponds with the biblical doctrine of **creation**, affirming that the world reflects God’s wisdom and purposeful design. It is not, by itself, the full Gospel. Knowing that God exists does not remove our sin or reconcile us to Him. We need Jesus Christ, the eternal Son who became man, died as a substitute for sinners, was buried, and bodily rose again. Turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone for forgiveness and eternal life.

question: What is the difference between the universal and local church?
answer:
The **universal church** is the whole body of genuinely saved believers in Christ across every age and place, while a **local church** is a particular congregation of believers who gather for worship, teaching, fellowship, the ordinances, and mutual accountability.

- **Universal church:** Christ’s entire redeemed people. “God put everything under His feet and made Him head over everything for the church, which is His body, the fullness of Him who fills all in all” (Ephesians 1:22–23; see also Matthew 16:18; Hebrews 12:22–24).
- **Local church:** A specific, identifiable congregation in a particular place. The New Testament addresses “the church of God in Corinth” (1 Corinthians 1:2), and describes believers gathering for teaching, fellowship, the breaking of bread, and prayer (Acts 2:42–47).

Some historic Christians use **“invisible church”** for the universal church and **“visible church”** for the local church, emphasizing that God alone perfectly knows who truly belongs to Christ, while the local congregation publicly recognizes professing believers. The distinction is useful, provided it does not minimize the local church, because Christ commands His people to gather, shepherd one another, observe baptism and the Lord’s Supper, and practice discipline (Matthew 28:19–20; 1 Corinthians 11:23–26; Hebrews 10:24–25).

In practical terms, every Christian belongs to the universal church by faith in Christ, and should ordinarily commit to a faithful local church where he or she can worship, receive biblical instruction, serve, and be cared for.

question: Why should I believe in God?
answer:
You should believe in God because He has made Himself known through creation, conscience, Scripture, and supremely through Jesus Christ. Christianity is not a blind leap into the dark, but a trusting response to God’s revelation.

Several reasons point toward God:

- **The universe points beyond itself.** Everything that begins has a cause, and the universe is not self-explanatory. The existence, order, and intelligibility of creation fit the biblical claim that it was made by a personal Creator: “In the beginning God created the heavens and the earth” (Genesis 1:1).
- **Moral obligation points to a moral Lawgiver.** We do not merely have preferences about justice, cruelty, or human dignity. We recognize that some things are truly right and wrong. Scripture teaches that God’s law is also reflected in human conscience (Romans 2:14–16).
- **Human personhood and reason point to more than matter.** Love, rational thought, beauty, meaning, and moral responsibility are difficult to account for if reality is only impersonal particles and forces. The Bible explains them by teaching that human beings are made in God’s image (Genesis 1:26–27).
- **God has spoken.** The Bible is not merely humanity’s speculation about God. It presents itself as inspired revelation, centered on God’s acts in history and fulfilled in Christ (2 Timothy 3:16–17; Hebrews 1:1–3).
- **Jesus is the decisive revelation.** Jesus Christ was truly God and truly man, lived without sin, died as a substitute for sinners, was buried, and bodily rose from the dead. The apostles proclaimed this as historical truth, not private religious experience: “He was delivered over to death for our trespasses and was raised to life for our justification” (Romans 4:25).

It is also fair to acknowledge why people struggle to believe. Suffering can make God’s goodness seem difficult to understand, and religious hypocrisy can make God’s people seem untrustworthy. Those concerns deserve honest answers. Yet neither suffering nor hypocrisy disproves God, and the Christian faith does not ignore suffering. At the cross, God Himself entered our grief and bore judgment for sin. The resurrection promises that death and evil will not have the final word.

The deepest issue is not simply whether enough evidence exists. Scripture says that sin has separated us from God and that we need a Savior, not merely more information (Romans 3:23; Ephesians 2:1–5). God is holy, and we cannot make ourselves acceptable through good works. But Jesus offers justification, being declared righteous before God, by grace alone through faith alone in Him.

Turn from your sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died on the cross and rose bodily for your forgiveness and new life. As you seek honestly, read the Gospel of John, ask God to show you the truth, and consider discussing your questions with a faithful local pastor or mature Christian. What most makes belief difficult for you, the question of evidence, the problem of suffering, or something personal?

question: How is the church the Body of Christ?
answer:
The church is called **the Body of Christ** because all who are united to Jesus by faith are spiritually joined to Him and to one another, as different members form one living body under one head. Christ is the **Head**, and the church is His people, indwelt and empowered by the Holy Spirit to represent Him and carry out His mission in the world.

Paul writes:

> “For just as each of us has one body with many members, and not all members have the same function, so in Christ we who are many are one body, and each member belongs to one another.”  
> **Romans 12:4–5**

This includes several truths:

- **Christ is the Head and Lord of the church.** He rules, nourishes, and directs His people: **Ephesians 1:22–23; Colossians 1:18**.
- **Believers are united to Christ by the Holy Spirit.** This union is not merely organizational. Through faith, Christians share in Christ’s life and belong to Him: **1 Corinthians 12:12–13**.
- **The church has many members with different gifts and roles.** No Christian is unnecessary, and no Christian is meant to live independently of the rest: **1 Corinthians 12:14–27**.
- **The church makes Christ known through its life and ministry.** The church does not become Christ or replace Him, but it is called to display His character, proclaim His gospel, serve others, and make disciples: **Matthew 28:18–20; Ephesians 4:15–16**.
- **The body is both universal and local.** All true believers belong to Christ’s universal church, while they ordinarily express that union through committed participation in a local congregation: **Acts 2:42–47; Hebrews 10:24–25**.

This image also gives a strong warning against division and selfishness. Since believers belong to one another, “if one member suffers, every other member suffers with it; if one member is honored, every other member rejoices with it” (**1 Corinthians 12:26**). Practically, this means committing yourself to a faithful local church, using your gifts to serve others, bearing burdens, receiving correction, and refusing to treat church life as optional Christianity.

The church is Christ’s body because He has redeemed it by His blood, united it to Himself by faith, and now sanctifies it by His Spirit. Its hope is that Christ will finally present it to Himself holy and glorious, without spot or wrinkle (**Ephesians 5:25–27**).

question: What are some undeniable examples of divine intervention?
answer:
“Undeniable” depends on what standard of evidence is being used. For Christians, God’s clearest and decisive intervention is not merely a surprising coincidence or private experience, but the public acts God has revealed in Scripture, especially the resurrection of Jesus Christ.

Examples include:

- **Creation itself:** God brought the heavens and earth into existence by His word, rather than being part of creation Himself. “In the beginning God created the heavens and the earth” (Genesis 1:1).
- **The exodus from Egypt:** God judged Egypt through the plagues, delivered Israel through the Red Sea, and established His covenant with His people (Exodus 7–14). This was presented as a public act witnessed by an entire nation.
- **The preservation of Daniel:** God shut the mouths of lions and preserved Daniel when he was thrown into the den (Daniel 6:19–23).
- **The incarnation and virgin birth:** The eternal Son truly entered human history as Jesus Christ, conceived by the Holy Spirit and born of the Virgin Mary (Matthew 1:18–25; John 1:1–14). This is the mystery of the **hypostatic union**, Christ being truly God and truly man.
- **Jesus’ miracles:** Christ healed the sick, forgave sins, commanded nature, cast out demons, and raised the dead. These signs testified that He is the Messiah and Son of God (Mark 2:1–12; John 11:38–44; John 20:30–31).
- **The bodily resurrection of Jesus:** Jesus was crucified, buried, and raised physically on the third day. This is the central divine intervention in history, confirming His deity, defeating death, and securing justification for His people (1 Corinthians 15:3–8, 17; Romans 4:25).
- **Pentecost and the birth of the church:** The risen Christ poured out the Holy Spirit, empowering the apostles to proclaim the Gospel and gathering people from many nations into one church (Acts 2:1–41).
- **The conversion of Saul of Tarsus:** A violent persecutor of Christians was confronted by the risen Christ and transformed into the apostle Paul (Acts 9:1–19; Galatians 1:13–16).

God also intervenes through **providence**, His ordinary and sovereign ordering of events, not only through miracles. A providential answer to prayer may be unmistakably precious to the person who receives it, yet it should be tested humbly by Scripture rather than treated as equal to biblical revelation. “Test all things. Hold fast to what is good” (1 Thessalonians 5:21).

The resurrection stands above all claimed signs because it is the foundation of the Christian faith: Christ’s death was the necessary **penal substitution** for sinners, and His bodily resurrection publicly demonstrated His victory over sin and death. Therefore, divine intervention is not merely that God occasionally changes circumstances. It is that God has entered His creation to save sinners through Jesus Christ.

Turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose again for forgiveness and new life.

question: What is the institutional church?
answer:
The **institutional church** is the organized, visible community of Christians gathered under Christ’s authority, with recognized leaders, teaching, worship, ordinances, membership, and discipline. It is not primarily a building or bureaucracy, but a local body of believers ordered according to Christ’s commands.

The New Testament presents the church as both:

- **The universal church**, all true believers united to Christ: “Christ is the head of the church, which is His body” (Ephesians 5:23).
- **The local church**, a visible congregation that gathers, appoints elders, receives members, practices baptism and the Lord’s Supper, teaches Scripture, and exercises discipline. See Matthew 18:15–20; Acts 2:41–42; Acts 14:23; 1 Corinthians 5:4–5; 1 Timothy 3:1–13.

The word *church* translates the Greek **ekklesia**, meaning an assembly or congregation. Thus, the institutional church is not separate from the spiritual church as though organization were unspiritual. Christ gives His people real structure and authority for their good. Elders shepherd the flock, members serve one another, and the whole congregation submits to God’s Word. See Acts 20:28; 1 Peter 5:1–4; Hebrews 13:17.

At the same time, an institution can become spiritually dead if it has outward form without genuine faith. Jesus warned about honoring God with the lips while the heart is far from Him (Matthew 15:7–9). The true church therefore requires both **visible order** and **living faith in Christ**.

Practically, a healthy institutional church should preach the whole counsel of Scripture, proclaim salvation by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone, administer baptism and the Lord’s Supper faithfully, appoint qualified elders, practice loving discipline, and cultivate genuine fellowship. A wise next step is to seek a local church where these marks are evident rather than choosing only by style, size, or convenience.

question: Is Christianity true?
answer:
Yes. Christianity is true because its central claims are grounded in God’s real acts in history, especially the incarnation, death, burial, and bodily resurrection of Jesus Christ.

You may reasonably wonder whether the resurrection is credible, whether the Bible has been faithfully transmitted, or whether Christianity is too exclusive. Christians do not believe merely because Christianity feels meaningful. We believe because God has revealed Himself, Jesus truly lived and died, the tomb was found empty, His disciples testified that they saw Him risen, and the apostolic message was proclaimed publicly from the beginning. Paul summarized the historical heart of the faith:

> “For I delivered to you first and foremost what I also received: that Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures, that He was buried, that He was raised on the third day according to the Scriptures, and that He appeared to Cephas and then to the Twelve.”  
> 1 Corinthians 15:3–5

The Bible teaches that Jesus is not merely a prophet or moral teacher. He is the eternal Son of God who became truly man, the truth revealed in the hypostatic union, one Person with fully divine and fully human natures. Jesus said, “I am the way and the truth and the life. No one comes to the Father except through Me” (John 14:6). His claims were confirmed by His works, His sinless life, His fulfillment of Scripture, and above all His bodily resurrection. The apostles declared, “God has raised this Jesus to life, to which we are all witnesses” (Acts 2:32).

Christianity is also true in what it says about us. God is holy, while we are sinners who cannot reconcile ourselves to Him through good works. “For all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God” (Romans 3:23). At the cross, Christ bore the judgment deserved by His people, which is **penal substitution**, and God justifies sinners by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone. “God proves His love for us in this: While we were still sinners, Christ died for us” (Romans 5:8).

So Christianity is not simply a system of ethics or private spirituality. It is the announcement that Jesus Christ is Lord, that He died for sins, was buried, rose bodily on the third day, and now reigns. Turn from your sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose for forgiveness and new life.

A wise place to begin is to read the Gospel of John carefully, asking God to show you who Jesus is, and to examine especially John 20:30–31. What part of Christianity’s truth claim most concerns or troubles you: the existence of God, the reliability of the Bible, the resurrection, or the exclusivity of Christ?

question: What is ministry?
answer:
Ministry is **serving God by serving people according to His Word, for the glory of Christ and the good of others**. The word means “service,” and every Christian is called to ministry, not only pastors or missionaries.

Jesus said, “The Son of Man did not come to be served, but to serve, and to give His life as a ransom for many” (Matthew 20:28). Christian ministry therefore begins with Christ’s own service, especially His **atoning death** on the cross, and flows from gratitude for salvation by grace through faith in Him.

Ministry includes:

- Proclaiming the gospel of Jesus Christ, including His death, burial, and bodily resurrection (1 Corinthians 15:3–4).
- Teaching and obeying God’s Word (Matthew 28:19–20).
- Encouraging, helping, and caring for fellow believers (Galatians 6:2; 1 Peter 4:10–11).
- Serving the needy and showing mercy (James 1:27).
- Using spiritual gifts to build up the church (Ephesians 4:11–13).
- Honoring God faithfully in ordinary callings, such as family, work, hospitality, and daily relationships (Colossians 3:17, 23–24).

The church has particular offices and public ministries, such as elders and deacons (1 Timothy 3:1–13), but ministry is not limited to ordained leaders. Every believer is a servant of Christ, and the Holy Spirit equips each member of Christ’s body for useful service (1 Corinthians 12:4–7).

A practical beginning is to pray, study Scripture, join faithfully with a local church, and ask mature believers where your gifts and opportunities can meet real needs. Ministry is not a way to earn God’s acceptance. It is the grateful fruit of justification, as we serve the Lord who first served and saved us.

question: What is classical apologetics?
answer:
Classical apologetics is a Christian approach to defending the truth of the faith by using reason, evidence, and the truths Christians share with unbelievers. It commonly proceeds in two stages: first, arguing that God exists, and then showing that Christianity is true through evidence for the reliability of Scripture, Jesus’ identity, His miracles, and His bodily resurrection.

The word *apologetics* comes from the Greek *apologia*, meaning a reasoned defense, as in 1 Peter 3:15: “But in your hearts sanctify Christ as Lord. Always be prepared to give an answer to everyone who asks you to explain the hope you have, but respond with gentleness and respect.”

A typical classical apologetic argument may look like this:

1. **God exists**, supported by arguments from causation, contingency, morality, or design.
2. **A theistic God can reveal Himself**, because a personal and intelligent Creator is capable of communication.
3. **The Bible’s revelation is trustworthy**, based on its historical claims, fulfilled prophecy, coherence, and preservation.
4. **Jesus is truly God and truly man**, confirmed especially by His claims, miracles, death, and resurrection.
5. **The bodily resurrection is historical**, providing the central confirmation of the Gospel: Christ died for sins, was buried, and rose on the third day, as stated in 1 Corinthians 15:3–8.

Classical apologetics is not meant to replace repentance or faith. Arguments can remove intellectual obstacles, but only the Holy Spirit gives spiritual sight and brings a sinner to saving faith. Salvation is by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone, because “faith comes by hearing, and hearing by the word of Christ” (Romans 10:17).

A major alternative is **presuppositional apologetics**, which argues that all reasoning depends on ultimate assumptions and that the triune God revealed in Scripture is necessary for intelligible thought, morality, and knowledge. Classical apologists generally begin with broadly shared reasoning and then argue toward Christianity, while presuppositional apologists emphasize that no one reasons from a truly neutral standpoint.

Classical apologetics can be a useful tool, especially when someone asks whether belief in God or the resurrection is rational, but the Christian’s goal is not merely to win an argument. It is to bear faithful witness to Jesus Christ, crucified and risen, with both truth and love.

question: Why does God allow birth defects?
answer:
Birth defects are heartbreaking, and it is right to ask why a good and powerful God allows them. Scripture does not give a simple explanation for every individual case, but it does give several firm truths.

First, a birth defect is not necessarily the result of that child’s or parents’ personal sin. When Jesus’ disciples asked whether a man’s blindness was caused by his sin or his parents’ sin, Jesus rejected that assumption: “Neither this man nor his parents sinned” (John 9:3). We should therefore refuse both blame and shame.

Second, the Bible teaches that creation is presently subjected to corruption because of humanity’s fall into sin. This does not mean that every particular disability can be traced to a particular act of sin, but it does mean that disease, weakness, and death belong to a world that is no longer as God originally made it. “The whole creation has been groaning together in the pains of childbirth until the present time” (Romans 8:22).

Third, God remains sovereign and good even when His purposes are hidden from us. Psalm 139:13-16 affirms God’s intimate knowledge and care for a child in the womb, while John 9 shows that God can display His works through circumstances that involve profound suffering. This does not make the suffering itself good, nor does it give us permission to speak casually about God’s hidden purposes. We should weep with those who weep, provide practical help, and trust God’s character when we cannot understand His providence.

The deepest Christian answer is not an explanation but a person: Jesus Christ. The Son of God entered our suffering, took on true humanity, and bore sin’s judgment through penal substitution on the cross. He was buried, bodily raised on the third day, and will return to remove every effect of sin and renew creation. In Christ, suffering is not meaningless, and disability is not the final definition of anyone’s worth. “He will wipe away every tear from their eyes. There will be no more death or mourning or crying or pain” (Revelation 21:4).

A practical response is to bring the grief honestly to God, seek wise medical care and support, and involve a faithful local church that will serve the child and family rather than offer blame. If this question is personal, you do not have to carry it alone. Turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose again for forgiveness, hope, and eternal life. What part of this question is most personal for you, the pain, the fairness of God, or fear about the future?

question: Why doesn't God heal everyone?
answer:
This is a painful question, especially when someone you love is suffering. The Bible teaches that God **can** heal, sometimes does heal, and invites us to ask Him for healing, but He has not promised to heal every illness in this present age.

Illness and death entered human experience through the fall into sin, so creation now groans under corruption. Yet sickness is not always a direct punishment for a particular person’s sin. Jesus rejected that simplistic conclusion when asked about a man born blind, saying, “This was not so that he and his parents sinned” (John 9:3).

Several truths help us hold this mystery:

- **God remains sovereign and good**, even when His purposes are hidden. “My thoughts are not your thoughts, neither are your ways My ways,” declares the LORD (Isaiah 55:8–9). We should not pretend to know the specific reason God permits a particular illness.
- **God may use suffering to refine and sustain His people**, though suffering itself is not good. Paul pleaded for the removal of his “thorn in the flesh,” but Christ answered, “My grace is sufficient for you, for My power is perfected in weakness” (2 Corinthians 12:7–10).
- **Healing is a sign of Christ’s kingdom, but its fullness is still future.** Jesus healed many as evidence that He is the Messiah, but even those people eventually died. Christians await the resurrection, when God will permanently remove death, mourning, crying, and pain (Revelation 21:3–4).
- **God Himself entered our suffering in Jesus Christ.** Christ is truly God and truly man, and He understands weakness and grief. At the cross, He bore sin’s judgment as our substitute, and His bodily resurrection guarantees that death will not have the final word (Hebrews 4:15–16; 1 Corinthians 15:3–4, 20–26).

So Christians should pray earnestly for healing, seek appropriate medical care, receive help from the church, and still entrust the outcome to God. James 5:14–16 calls believers to pray for the sick, while Philippians 1:20–24 reminds us that whether by continued life or by death, Christ remains our hope.

A practical next step is to pray honestly through Psalm 13 or Psalm 23, naming your pain, asking for healing, and asking God for grace to trust Him one day at a time; also share your burden with mature believers and your church elders rather than carrying it alone.

If you have not yet come to Christ, the deepest human problem is not sickness but sin and separation from a holy God. Jesus died on the cross for sinners, was buried, rose bodily on the third day, and now reigns as Lord. Turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone for forgiveness, reconciliation with God, and everlasting life.

question: What does it mean that the Bible is self-authenticating?
answer:
The Bible is **self-authenticating** because, as God’s inspired Word, it bears God’s own authority and displays divine qualities that testify to its origin. Its authority does not come from the church, a council, historical scholarship, or human approval. The church recognizes Scripture as God’s Word, but it does not make Scripture God’s Word.

This does **not** mean that Christians must ignore evidence, history, manuscripts, or the witness of the early church. Such evidence can confirm and strengthen confidence in the Bible, but it cannot be the ultimate foundation of its authority. If something outside the Bible had to give Scripture its final authority, that outside standard would actually be more authoritative than God’s Word.

The Bible’s self-authentication includes three closely related truths:

- **Scripture claims divine origin:** “All Scripture is God-breathed and is useful for instruction, for conviction, for correction, and for training in righteousness” (2 Timothy 3:16).
- **Scripture possesses divine qualities:** It is truthful, powerful, coherent, morally holy, spiritually discerning, and able to expose the human heart: “For the word of God is living and active, sharper than any double-edged sword” (Hebrews 4:12).
- **The Holy Spirit inwardly confirms it:** Fallen human beings do not naturally welcome God’s truth, so the Spirit opens the mind and heart to recognize Scripture as God’s voice. “The one who belongs to God hears what God says” (John 8:47). Compare also 1 Corinthians 2:12–14; 1 Thessalonians 2:13.

This is sometimes called the **internal testimony of the Holy Spirit**. It is not merely a private feeling or an irrational leap. Rather, the Spirit enables believers to perceive Scripture’s divine authority through Scripture itself, much as a healthy eye recognizes light. The Spirit does not add new revelation to the Bible, but illumines what God has already given.

There is an unavoidable kind of circularity here, but it is not uniquely a Christian problem. Every ultimate authority must finally appeal to itself. A person who says that human reason, science, personal experience, or the church is the final authority must also use that authority to validate itself. The Christian claim is that God’s Word is the highest authority, so it cannot be judged by a higher standard. Scripture says, “The words of the LORD are flawless, like silver refined in a furnace, like gold purified sevenfold” (Psalm 12:6).

In short, **the Bible is authenticated by God through its own divine character and the Holy Spirit’s witness, while historical and external evidence serves as confirmation rather than the source of its authority**. This gives Christians confidence to receive Scripture not merely as an ancient religious document, but “as the word of God,” which is “truly at work in you who believe” (1 Thessalonians 2:13).
